  - Set up a Tenant Decarbonisation Partnership (TDP) programme with green lease clauses, data sharing, and co-investment mechanisms (service charge or recovery via green rent).

- Funding
  - Allocate £55m/year capex across three tranches: compliance-critical (40%), value-uplift deep retrofits (45%), innovation/contingency (15%).
  - Layer green loans/sustainability-linked RCF, EPC/heat network grants (Boiler Upgrade Scheme for ASHPs/GSHPs, PSDS equivalent where eligible), and rooftop PV Smart Export Guarantee revenues.

2) Portfolio diagnostics and phasing
- Asset segmentation (A/B/C)
  - A) Quick wins: EPC C/D assets with strong fabric, simple HVAC—upgrade to B by 2027.
  - B) Core deep-retrofit candidates: offices with gas boilers/CHP and poor controls; retail parades with F/G EPC—target by 2030.
  - C) Complex mixed-use with shared plant/resi above retail—bundle into multi-year projects concluding by 2032–2034.

- Metering and data
  - Mandate AMR/sub-metering across all end-uses within 18 months.
  - Implement a single data platform for landlord and tenant energy, refrigerants, and water; automate SECR and SBTi tracking.
  - Rolling M&V per IPMVP Option B/C for major retrofits.

3) Technical pathway by asset type
- Offices (180,000 m2)
  - 2025–2027: Controls-led savings (15–20%)
    - BMS upgrades, smart scheduling, fault detection, demand-controlled ventilation, heat recovery, LED and daylighting, plug load management.
  - 2026–2032: Electrify heat and hot water
    - Replace gas boilers/CHP with high-temperature air-to-water heat pumps (HTHP) or hybrid ASHP + thermal storage; consider shared GSHP borefields where sites allow.
    - Fabric upgrades at time of major works: roof/wall insulation, air-tightness; glazing to low-e double/triple where cost-effective.
  - 2026–2030: Ventilation/comfort and IAQ modernisation to protect prime rents; ensure NABERS UK star targets (≥4.5 by 2030).
  - 2025–2030: On-site PV and behind-the-meter batteries where roof load and grid constraints permit; integrate EV charging with load management.

- Retail (95,000 m2) with 30% F/G risk
  - 2025–2026: Immediate EPC compliance sweep
    - LED, HVAC tune-ups, heat pump RTUs where feasible, destratification fans, refrigeration case doors, heat reclaim; door curtains/vestibules.
    - Refrigerant strategy: phase down high-GWP gases (R404A/R410A) to R454B/CO2; leak detection; tenant engagement for display fridges and split systems.
  - 2026–2029: Fabric and plant
    - Package rooftop ASHP units, variable-speed drives, improved controls with sub-tenant metering.
    - For parades with residential above, decouple flues; upgrade envelopes where landlord has rights; otherwise offer tenant incentives plus green lease triggers at lease events.
  - 2025–2028: Contractual levers
    - Make green clauses standard: minimum fit-out energy standards, refrigerant specs, disclosure of interval data, limits on electric resistance heating, LED-only policy.

- Build-to-Rent (1,200 units)
  - 2025–2027: No-gas policy for replacements; heat pumps for DHW (centralised with thermal stores) or individual ASHPs in flats; smart TRVs and heat cost allocators.
  - 2026–2030: Where central plant serves mixed-use, migrate to ambient loop with distributed water-to-water heat pumps; recover low-grade heat from retail refrigeration/AC condensers.
  - Resident engagement: in-app nudges, real-time usage, green tariffs default opt-in; EPC B/A uplift via fabric and glazing at lifecycle events.

4) Cross-cutting decarbonisation levers
- Heat electrification roadmap
  - 2025: Freeze any new gas plant; all replacements must be heat-pump ready.
  - 2026–2032: Staged boiler retirements aligned with lifecycle, targeting 100% removal by 2032. Buffer tanks and thermal stores to flatten peaks.
  - Evaluate city heat networks (Manchester, Birmingham): connect only if low-carbon factor is verifiable and contractual decarbonisation is guaranteed.

- Renewable electricity procurement
  - 2025–2027: Shift to 100% market-based renewable electricity for landlord meters (REGOs), prioritising UK-sited assets.
  - 2027–2030: Add long-term utility PPAs (sleeved) for additionality; size ~70–80% of predictable office/landlord load, hedge residual with REGO.
  - On-site PV on all viable roofs; community solar where roofs are constrained; share benefits with tenants via private wire where legally/technically feasible.

- Refrigerants
  - Inventory all systems by 2025; cut fugitive emissions >50% by 2028 through replacements and enhanced maintenance.
  - Specify low-GWP refrigerants in all new/replacement systems and adopt leak detection/automatic shut-off.

- Embodied carbon
  - Retrofit-first policy; PAS 2080-aligned assessments for major works.
  - Low-carbon materials (A2A cement substitutes, recycled steel/aluminium), and reuse of fit-out components; track kgCO2e/m2 targets for interventions.

5) Regulation, risk and compliance
- EPC and MEES
  - 2025–2028: Eradicate F/G in retail tranche; minimum E by 2026 and C by 2028 as a safe harbour against likely tightening; reach B portfolio average by 2030.
  - Create an EPC “landing plan” for every unit; use lease breaks/renewals to mandate upgrades.

- Building regs and operational performance
  - Anticipate shift to operational ratings (NABERS UK/DECs for offices). Commit to public disclosure of office operational energy by 2027.
  - Maintain UKGBC Net Zero Carbon Framework alignment for in-use.

- Grid and capacity
  - Early DNO engagement for heat pump and EV loads; deploy demand response, thermal storage, and staged connections to avoid grid delays.

- Tenant dependencies
  - Implement green lease schedule with:
    - Data sharing as a condition precedent
    - Fit-out energy and refrigerant standards
    - Cost-recovery mechanisms for LL-funded base building upgrades where tenant benefits accrue
    - Service-charge treatment for energy-saving capex where statute permits
  - Create a tenant retrofit incentive fund offering co-funding for high-impact measures (e.g., refrigeration doors).

- Market and valuation
  - Use discounted cash flow scenarios reflecting brown discount for non-compliant assets and green premium for NABERS/EPRA sBPR-leading assets to prioritise capex.
  - Consider selective disposals of hard-to-decarbonise, short-WALE, fragmented retail with costly structural constraints.

6) Capex, savings, and emissions trajectory (order-of-magnitude)
- Baseline Scope 1+2: 42 ktCO2e/yr (shared plant to be carefully allocated)
- 2025–2027: Controls/LED/quick wins and RE electricity
  - Capex: ~£35–45m/yr portion
  - Emissions reduction: 35–45% (to ~23–27 kt)
  - Eliminate F/G to <5% of retail by end-2027
- 2026–2032: Heat electrification + fabric + PV
  - Capex: ~£55–60m/yr average
  - Additional reduction: 40–50% (to ~10–14 kt)
- 2032–2035: Final optimisation, residuals, hard-to-reach tenants
  - Capex: ~£30–40m/yr
  - Residuals: ~3–4 kt (primarily tenant-driven and refrigerants)
- Offsets/neutralisation from 2035
  - Only for residuals with high-quality, durable removal credits; publish abatement hierarchy.

7) Mixed-tenure complexity: practical solutions
- Governance of shared plant
  - Where retail and resi share plant, establish cost/risk-sharing agreements and metering to allocate consumption; prioritise central plant upgrades that decouple uses via ambient loops.
- Legal levers
  - Add alteration rights for fabric upgrades affecting retail frontages and resi above; standardise deed of variation templates to streamline consent.
- Programme scheduling
  - Bundle units by vertical stack per scheme to minimise disruption and scaffold costs; use seasonal windows for intrusive works.

8) KPIs and reporting
- Annual targets
  - -8 to -10% Scope 1+2 intensity per year to 2030; ≥90% reduction by 2035.
  - EPC distribution: 0% F/G by 2028; ≥80% B or better by 2030.
  - 100% landlord RE electricity by 2027; ≥60% additional via PPAs by 2030.
  - 100% of leases on green clauses by next event; 90% tenant data coverage by 2027.
  - Fugitive emissions: -50% by 2028; -80% by 2032.
- Disclosure
  - EPRA sBPR, SECR, TCFD, and SBTi validation for near-term target by 2026; long-term net zero target reiterated.

9) Immediate next 12-month actions
- Commission detailed heat decarbonisation studies for top 10 emitters; create asset-level roadmaps with costed options and EPC landing plans.
- Switch landlord electricity to certified renewables and commence PPA procurement.
- Launch tenant data and green lease programme; pilot two retail retrofits tackling refrigeration and RTU replacement.
- Procure framework partners for heat pumps, controls, PV, and M&V; start DNO applications.
- Establish the NZDO, set carbon budgets, and integrate KPIs into asset managers’ scorecards.

This pathway reduces compliance risk, sequences capex to protect cash flows, aligns with SBTi 1.5°C, and manages the mixed-use dependencies that typically stall delivery.

Here’s a pragmatic, fund‑level net zero pathway for a secondary UK regional office portfolio with tight capex (~1.2% real p.a.), material obsolescence risk (avg EPC E; 18 F/G), and some assets likely to be disposed. It focuses on value preservation, compliance, and emissions reduction, with clear triage between Retain/Refurbish vs Dispose, and staged sequencing to 2050.

1) Portfolio triage and strategy envelope (0–12 months)
- Segment assets into four buckets using a simple scorecard (location demand/lettability, building fabric and services, EPC/MEES risk, floorplate efficiency, capex intensity to hit EPC B/C, lease profile, and yield on cost).  
  A. Core Retain/Refurbish: Stronger regional cities/micro‑locations, good bones (structure, floor-to-ceiling, cores), viable to EPC B by 2030 with moderate capex.  
  B. Transitional/Selective: OK locations but heavier lifts; target EPC C by 2030, defer to B by 2035–2040; consider partial repositioning or change-of-use options.  
  C. Hold-to-Dispose: Market or physical constraints; invest only to de-risk legal compliance and liquidity (reach EPC E/C where needed) and sell into improving liquidity windows.  
  D. Exit/Semi-stranded: Poor locations, deep retrofit cost >> value; plan accelerated disposal or repurpose exploration with partners; avoid major capex.
- Initial targets and constraints:  
  - Keep average annual net capex near 1.2% of portfolio value, flexing to 2–3% in clustered “retrofit years” for A/B buckets funded by sales from C/D.  
  - Set an ex-ante capex-to-carbon abatement threshold (e.g., <£150–£200/tCO2e to 2030 for Scope 1+2).  
  - Emissions glidepath: -50% Scope 1+2 by 2030 vs baseline 65 ktCO2e; near-zero operational by 2040; residuals offset/neutralized by 2050.  
  - Vacancy strategy: Use high-vacancy assets in A/B as early decant sites to enable intrusive works.

2) Compliance and risk baseline (next 6–12 months)
- Regulations to anchor:  
  - MEES: Non-domestic lettings currently require EPC E or better; government consultation signalled EPC B by 2030 (though timelines uncertain). Do not rely on slippage—assume EPC C by 2027 staging to B by 2030–2033 for planning.  
  - UK ETS/heat decarbonisation: Expect rising carbon and heat policy pressure; early removal of fossil boilers reduces stranded risk.  
  - Energy/Building regs: Anticipate Part L tightening; metering/submetering, TM44, F-gas phase-down, refrigerant transitions.  
  - Local planning: Some cities push operational energy disclosure and embodied carbon plans for major refurbishments.  
- Data foundation: roll out AMR/submetering to >80% of floor area within 12 months; implement a utility data platform; conduct Level 2 energy audits for all A/B, Level 1 for C/D; produce EPC/DEC refresh for all assets by month 12.

3) Pathway by bucket

A) Core Retain/Refurbish (c. 25–35 assets; ~50–60% of area; bulk of emissions)
- Objective: EPC B by 2030–2033; operational energy intensity to NABERS UK 4.5–5 star equivalent by 2035; electrified heat by 2035.  
- Sequencing:  
  1. Quick wins (2026–2027):  
     - LED + controls, VSDs, BMS recommissioning, setback schedules, airtightness fixes; lift standby optimisations.  
     - Heat zoning, TRVs, valve balancing, condenser/boiler tuning; data layer + M&V.  
     - On renewal, green leases (energy data sharing, no-fossil replacements, fit-out efficiency clauses).  
     - Target 10–15% energy cut with <2-year paybacks.  
  2. Envelope and systems (2027–2030):  
     - Replace end-of-life boilers with heat pumps (where feasible) or hybrid interim; electrify DHW; upgrade AHUs with EC fans/heat recovery; demand-controlled ventilation.  
     - Façade upgrades prioritised on worst performers: glazing replacement or secondary glazing, external insulation where planning allows; roof insulation upgrades.  
     - Lift to EPC C/B as required; coordinate with lease events to reduce downtime.  
  3. Full electrification and deep optimisation (2030–2035):  
     - Complete heat pump rollout; remove gas; optimise low-temp distribution; thermal storage where it supports tariff shifting.  
     - Onsite PV on suitable roofs; PPAs for residual electricity; battery only if tariffs/storage value stack supports.  
- Dependencies: grid capacity checks before electrification; planning for façade; tenant engagement for after-hours reductions and heat pump operating temps.  
- Capex approach: stage works at natural lease breaks; bundle M&E replacements; use performance contracts for metered savings.  
- Emissions impact: 35–45% reduction by 2030 from A-bucket alone; 60–70% by 2035 with electrification + green procurement.

B) Transitional/Selective (c. 15–20 assets; ~25–30% area)
- Objective: EPC C by 2027–2030; defer EPC B to 2035–2040 where economics depend on market recovery or planning.  
- Actions:  
  - Immediate compliance lifts: plant upgrades with EPC lift in mind (LED, controls, limited façade works); prepare “no‑regrets” provisions for future heat pumps (oversize risers, electrical capacity, emitters sized for low flow temps).  
  - Pilot two deep retrofits to test cost, tenant response, and valuation uplift in secondary markets.  
  - Consider partial conversions (flex, labs where clusters exist, or residential where policy supports); run feasibility including embodied carbon and value.  
- Disposal option: If pilot fails to demonstrate yield on cost within hurdle, reclassify to C or D and time sale.

C) Hold-to-Dispose (c. 8–12 assets; ~10–15% area)
- Objective: Maintain lettability and legal compliance; avoid heavy capex; sell into windows 2027–2030 and 2032–2035.  
- Actions:  
  - Target EPC E→D/C with low-cost measures: LED, controls, limited boiler tuning or condensing replacements only if required for leaseability.  
  - Cosmetic refresh to reduce vacancy and signal ESG progress; secure short leases to underpin income but preserve buyer flexibility.  
  - Prepare comprehensive vendor due diligence pack (EPC, audits, capex plan, ESG data) to support pricing and shorten execution time.  
- Risk guardrails: exit before EPC B mandate crystallises locally; avoid gas plant replacement that locks in 15-year fossil life beyond 2035.

D) Exit/Semi-stranded (c. 3–6 assets; ~5% area)
- Objective: Capital recovery or repurpose.  
- Actions:  
  - Early sale “as is” to value-add buyers; or pursue change-of-use JV where town-centre/resi viable.  
  - Limit spend to H&S and statutory compliance.  
- Timing: Aim disposals 2026–2028 while MEES tightening risk is not fully priced in, using improved data packs to support buyer underwriting.

4) Fund-level capex, financing, and sequencing
- Capex phasing:  
  - 2026–2028: Majority to A-bucket quick wins and C-bucket compliance lifts; 0.8–1.2% p.a.  
  - 2028–2033: Peak spend for A-bucket systems/façade and pilots in B; 1.5–3% p.a., funded by disposals from C/D and potential green debt.  
  - 2033–2038: Electrification completion; 1–1.5% p.a.  
- Funding levers: green loans linked to EPC uplift; CPPA-backed onsite/offsite renewables; performance contracting/ESCOs; explore LA/public funds or UKIB for deep retrofits in regeneration zones.  
- Protecting NOI: align works to lease events; use rent-free in lieu of disruption; market as “low‑cost to run” to drive faster lease-up; implement service charge recovery where leases allow for efficiency upgrades that reduce occupier costs.

5) Emissions pathway and energy strategy
- Scope 1+2 glidepath (indicative):  
  - 2026 baseline: 65 ktCO2e.  
  - 2028: -15–20% via O&M and quick wins, green procurement pilots.  
  - 2030: -45–55% with A-bucket EPC B/C and partial electrification; procure REGO‑backed electricity with quality screening.  
  - 2035: -70–80% with portfolio-wide electrification in A and part of B; offsite renewables PPAs for >70% of electricity.  
  - 2040: -90% operational with residual gas only in laggards; remaining emissions addressed via high-quality carbon removals from 2040+, tapering by 2050.  
- Energy procurement:  
  - Short term: green tariffs with additionality criteria and half-hourly data.  
  - Medium term: aggregated sleeved CPPAs for 30–50% load; layer spot + battery where demand charges justify.  
  - Demand flexibility: enable DR participation post‑BMS upgrades; thermal storage/hot water buffers on HP sites.

6) Key dependencies and enablers
- Grid capacity: early DNO engagement for HP rollouts; secure capacity letters and plan staged connections; consider shared services in multi-asset clusters.  
- Supply chain: framework agreements for HPs, LEDs, controls; pre‑approved product lists; contractor panels outside London to cap cost inflation.  
- Data and M&V: standardised submetering, analytics, and monthly performance reviews; meter-based incentives for FM.  
- Tenant alignment: green lease clauses, fit‑out guides (CAT A/B electrification ready), landlord-tenant committees; submetered billing transparency to drive behaviour.  
- Valuation proof points: track rental tone and void reduction post‑upgrades; document energy intensity and EPC uplifts to support yield compression arguments.

7) Regulatory and market risks to monitor
- MEES tightening to EPC B by 2030–33: non-compliance can strand leases and impair value; prioritise F/G and E assets in A/B for immediate uplift.  
- Heat policy shifts (boiler phase-out dates, heat network zoning): could accelerate forced electrification; avoid new long-life gas plant.  
- Grid decarbonisation trajectory: slower-than-expected decarb raises residual emissions; hedge with additionality-focused PPAs.  
- Disclosure regimes (SDR/ISSB, TCFD): ensure credible targets, data integrity, and audit trails to avoid greenwashing risk.  
- Rents vs retrofit cost in secondary markets: monitor letting evidence; if refurbishment premiums fail to materialise, fast-track disposals.  
- Embodied carbon scrutiny: for deep façade works, compare refurbishment vs redevelopment; document carbon payback to support planning and ESG claims.

8) Governance and milestones
- Year 1: triage complete; EPC refresh; data platform live; 100% audit coverage; all F/G moved to at least E/C plans with budget; first quick‑wins implemented.  
- By 2028: >80% of A/B to EPC C or better; 20–30% of A to B; portfolio emissions -20–30%.  
- By 2030–2033: All retained assets EPC B or clear plan/variance; emissions -50%+; CPPAs covering 30–50% load.  
- By 2035: Electrification substantially complete for A; -70–80% emissions; clear stance on any remaining C/D.  
- 2040: Operational near‑zero; residual offsets planned with removals.  
- Review annually: revisit bucket assignments, capex pacing, and disposal timing; update pathway with market and regulatory changes.

This plan preserves capital by focusing deep works where leasing and value support them, exits early from likely stranding risks, and sequences compliance, electrification, and procurement to meet a credible 2050 net zero commitment within the fund’s capex constraints.

Below is a pragmatic, lab‑aware net zero operational carbon pathway to 2040 for a UK REIT with life‑science campuses, recognising high lab loads, regulatory constraints, and portfolio heterogeneity. It prioritises demand reduction that preserves research quality, deep electrification, low‑carbon thermal solutions suited to 24/7, 100% OA operation, and credible residuals. It assumes c.£40m/year capex with phasing to 2040, and alignment to SBTi NZ Standard (Corporate Net-Zero Standard) and UK Net Zero Carbon Buildings Standard (NZCBS when final).

1) Governance, targets, and guardrails
- Target framework
  - SBTi near‑term target to 2030: ≥50% absolute Scope 1+2 reduction from 2023 baseline (38 ktCO2e/yr), covering all landlord‑controlled energy; commit to long‑term net zero by 2040 for operational carbon.
  - Separate intensity KPIs: kWh/m2 for office, kWh/m2 NIA for labs, and kWh/MEP point (e.g., per fume cupboard, per ULT freezer) to avoid load‑shift masking.
  - Whole‑building approach: include tenant plug/process loads where the REIT specifies/controls base build, central plant and BMS; use green lease clauses to extend scope and data visibility.
- Data and verification
  - Mandate half‑hourly metering granularity at plant, floor, and major end‑use (HVAC, process cooling, DHW, landlord vs tenant). 100% submeters by 2027.
  - Portfolio‑wide NABERS UK Energy for Offices and developing NABERS Labs or equivalent performance rating once available; use Design for Performance on new/major refurb.
  - Independent assurance annually; publish decarbonisation trajectory and CapEx plans site‑by‑site.
- Design standards (apply to new build and major refurb from 2026)
  - All‑electric base‑build; no new fossil boilers; no new gas CHP.
  - LEV/fume cupboard specifications to support low‑flow operation, VAV/AVC, and night‑setback; ULT freezer efficient classes; process heat recovery integrated.
  - Ventilation: demand‑controlled ventilation (DCV) with occupancy/process sensing; 100% OA with high‑efficiency energy recovery (run‑around coils/enthalpy wheels) where contamination risk can be managed.

2) Phased pathway to 2040
Phase 1: Stabilise, measure, and quick wins (2024–2026)
- Metering, BMS and analytics
  - Campus‑wide submeter rollout and analytics platform; fault detection and diagnostics (FDD).
  - BMS re‑commissioning; lab pressurisation cascade verification; calibrate sensors.
- HVAC optimisation without risk to safety
  - Implement DCV in office and non‑critical lab/support spaces; tighten turndown during unoccupied periods for eligible labs.
  - Rebalance airflows; set and enforce air change per hour (ACH) bands per lab risk class, targeting 4–6 ACH for many low‑hazard labs (vs legacy 10–12), per CIBSE/HTM guidance and local risk assessments.
  - Heat recovery audits; add coil bypass controls; repair failed heat exchangers; increase heat recovery effectiveness to 65–75% where safe.
- Fume cupboards
  - Inventory and classify; convert constant‑volume to VAV with occupancy/sash sensors; fit auto‑sash closers; training and dashboards (“Shut the Sash”).
  - Target 20–30% reduction in exhaust volume per upgraded cupboard; prioritise the top 20% of energy users.
- Process loads
  - ULT freezer management: consolidate, adopt −70°C where validated, specify <10 kWh/day units, add night‑setback in compatible models.
  - Autoclaves: heat recovery on condensate, schedule to off‑peak, high‑efficiency models at replacement.
- Electrification groundwork
  - Feasibility for low‑temperature ambient heat networks and central heat pumps at each campus; identify borehole/WSHP/rivers/condensers and reject heat sinks.
  - Grid capacity studies with DNOs; apply for capacity where constraints exist (Stevenage, Cambridge science parks often constrained).
- Procurement
  - Execute 100% renewable electricity supply with additionality pathway: move from standard REGOs to long‑term utility‑PPA or on‑site/off‑site PPAs by 2028; document incremental impact per SBTi guidance.
- Expected outcomes 2026
  - 10–15% portfolio kWh reduction; 12–18% Scope 1+2 reduction versus baseline.
  - CapEx: ~£15–20m/year focused on controls, metering, fume cupboard VAV retrofits, minor heat recovery.

Phase 2: Deep demand reduction and first-wave electrification (2026–2030)
- Ventilation and heat recovery at scale
  - Retrofit high‑efficiency energy recovery to AHUs serving eligible labs (run‑around or sensible wheels with purge sections to address contamination); target 70–80% effectiveness.
  - Night and weekend turndown for low/medium‑risk labs based on validated protocols; integrate occupancy and process sensors.
- Thermal systems
  - Replace end‑of‑life gas boilers with modular air‑to‑water heat pumps (AWHP) and/or water‑source (open/closed loop depending on site hydrogeology). Pair with low‑temp distribution (45–55°C).
  - Campus ambient loop approach: 10–25°C water loop interconnecting buildings; building‑level heat pumps lift to space heating/DHW; connect process cooling to dump reclaimable heat.
  - Heat recovery from process cooling, data rooms, autoclaves to pre‑heat DHW and primary loops.
- Electrical
  - Expand LV/HV infrastructure for heat pumps; install thermal and electrical storage (hot water buffers, phase‑change tanks; limited Li‑ion where needed for demand management).
- On‑site generation
  - PV on all viable roofs/facades/car‑ports; target 10–20% site consumption where geometry allows; consider behind‑the‑meter PPAs with tenants for process loads.
- Labs and equipment
  - Standardise Green Lab fit‑out specs: VAV cupboards ≤0.3 m/s face velocity in setback, containment verification, interlocks; specify high‑efficiency fans and ECM motors.
  - Replace legacy deep‑well pumps, vacuum pumps with dry scroll, variable‑speed units.
- Procurement and PPAs
  - Execute at least one long‑term off‑site wind/solar PPA covering 40–60% electricity; keep residual on certified renewable supply while additional PPA ramps.
- Expected outcomes 2030
  - 35–45% absolute Scope 1+2 reduction vs baseline; majority of office/support buildings electrified; 20–30% kWh/m2 reduction in labs that underwent ventilation optimisation.
  - CapEx: ~£40–50m/year peak as heat pumps and AHU retrofits scale.

Phase 3: Portfolio-wide electrification, residual minimisation (2030–2035)
- Complete fossil phase‑out
  - Decommission remaining gas boilers; connect remaining buildings to ambient loops; deploy larger central heat pumps with river/ground‑source where sites allow (Cambridge/Oxford aquifer potential).
  - Electrify humidification via adiabatic/ultrasonic where IAQ allows; electric steam generators where needed with heat recovery.
- Ventilation resilience
  - Upgrade critical labs to next‑gen energy recovery (sorbent wheels with purge, membrane exchangers) where cross‑contamination risk management is proven; expand DCV to high‑hazard with process‑linked controls.
- Temperature setpoints and zoning
  - Broaden acceptable bands in corridors and write‑up spaces; decouple office/write‑up from lab AHUs to avoid over‑ventilation.
- Digital and flexibility
  - Campus energy management with model‑predictive control, dynamic tariffs, participation in flexibility markets (DSR); size thermal storage to shift heat pump operation to low‑carbon hours.
- Tenant alignment
  - Green leases mandate equipment standards (ULT, autoclaves, fume cupboards), data sharing, and set change‑out timelines; offer landlord‑funded/tenant‑repayable upgrade programs.
- Expected outcomes 2035
  - 60–70% absolute Scope 1+2 reduction; residual Scope 1 close to zero; electricity consumption partially offset by PPAs and on‑site PV; operational ratings NABERS 4.5–5.5 stars for offices and high‑performing labs.

Phase 4: 2040 net zero operational carbon, high‑residuals strategy (2035–2040)
- Final increments
  - Address stubborn loads: 24/7 critical labs with high ACH/fume cupboard density; deploy next‑gen low‑pressure drop ductwork, ultra‑premium motors, and AI‑orchestrated sash control.
  - Replace any remaining steam generation with high‑efficiency electric and maximise heat recovery.
- Electricity decarbonisation and residual management
  - Ensure 100% electricity from additional renewable sources (PPAs + on‑site) that meet SBTi’s quality criteria; maintain location‑based reductions as grid decarbonises.
  - Residual balancing only after deep reductions: high‑quality carbon removals (durable, verified, limited volume) to neutralise any remaining operational emissions per SBTi guidance.

3) Technical measures summary for lab constraints
- Ventilation and fume cupboards
  - VAV and low‑flow technology, sash discipline, auto‑closers, occupancy sensors.
  - DCV with IAQ/process sensors; validated turndown schedules; segregation of high‑hazard labs to avoid penalising entire floors.
  - High‑efficiency heat recovery with contamination controls; purge sections or run‑around loops to avoid cross‑contamination.
- Heat pumps and heat recovery
  - Ambient loop architecture enabling simultaneous heating/cooling and process heat scavenging.
  - Source selection per site: WSHP (rivers/groundwater) at Cambridge/Oxford where feasible; ASHP with defrost strategies elsewhere; integrate with adiabatic dry coolers.
  - DHW via high‑temp heat pumps or cascade to 65–70°C for Legionella control; store at high temp, distribute at lower.
- Controls and analytics
  - FDD for fan power anomalies, sash open alarms, ACH drift.
  - Model predictive control linked to weather and tariffs; thermal storage dispatch to low‑carbon hours.
- Equipment standards and plug loads
  - Procurement policy for lab equipment energy performance; shared ULT banks; freezer farms with heat recovery; point‑of‑use DI/RO with recirc efficiency.
- Envelope only where it matters
  - Target air‑tightness and thermal bridging on refurb/new build; solar control glazing on office/write‑up areas; for labs, prioritise services efficiency over deep envelope retrofits unless major refurb.

4) Capex planning and sequencing (indicative)
- 2024–2026: metering, controls, VAV retrofits, AHU repairs, heat recovery add‑ons (£15–25m/yr).
- 2026–2030: first-wave heat pumps, ambient loops pilots, PV, major AHU replacements (£40–50m/yr).
- 2030–2035: portfolio electrification completion, storage, advanced energy recovery, tenant programs (£35–45m/yr).
- 2035–2040: optimisation, replacements at end of life, residual removal purchases (£25–35m/yr).
Leverage Salix/UKIB/green loans; consider heat‑as‑a‑service or ESCO models for campus loops.

5) Regulatory and market risks, mitigations
- Building regs and performance standards
  - England Part L uplift and potential operational performance standards (NABERS‑style) could tighten. Mitigation: adopt NABERS/design‑for‑performance now; electrify early to avoid stranded gas plant.
- MEES tightening
  - EPC B/C to A likely by 2030s; although portfolio EPC is B, labs risk EPC hits after electrotechnical changes. Mitigation: model EPC pre‑works; ensure efficient heat pump COPs and recoveries are reflected; document lab exemptions if applicable.
- Air quality and biosafety compliance
  - Changes to COSHH, HSE guidance, BS EN 14175 could constrain DCV/ACH reduction. Mitigation: risk‑assessed ventilation strategies signed off by competent person; maintain containment factors; separate high‑hazard spaces.
- Grid capacity constraints and connections
  - DNO queue delays can stall electrification. Mitigation: early applications, flexible connection offers, on‑site generation, storage, staged heat pump deployment, and demand flexibility revenues to offset costs.
- Renewable claims and SBTi scrutiny
  - Market‑based accounting via REGOs alone may not satisfy stakeholders. Mitigation: PPAs with additionality, publish location‑based and market‑based figures, disclose incremental impact.
- Tenant alignment risk
  - Tenants can undermine performance via equipment and operational practices. Mitigation: green leases, service charge recovery for upgrades, landlord‑provided compliant equipment options, training, and performance dashboards.
- Technology and refrigerant risk
  - F‑gas phase‑down will restrict high‑GWP refrigerants. Mitigation: select lower‑GWP (R290/R1234ze/R32 where appropriate), design for leak detection, and future refrigerant drop‑in where possible.
- Health/wellbeing
  - Thermal comfort, IAQ, and noise with lower‑temp systems. Mitigation: early design, appropriate coils, dehumidification strategies, and acoustic treatments; use TM59/TM52 checks.

6) KPIs and milestones
- 2026: 100% submeters; 15% Scope 1+2 reduction; ≥1 campus pilot ambient loop; 25% of fume cupboards on VAV/auto‑sash.
- 2030: 40–50% Scope 1+2 reduction; 70% of AHUs with energy recovery; all new works all‑electric; ≥50% electricity via PPA.
- 2035: 60–70% Scope 1+2 reduction; 90% buildings electrified; all fume cupboards VAV/auto‑sash or low‑flow; all labs on DCV where permissible.
- 2040: 90%+ absolute reduction vs baseline; residuals neutralised with high‑quality removals; third‑party verified net zero operational carbon.

7) Site‑specific notes (indicative)
- Cambridge/Oxford: investigate groundwater/river WSHPs and seasonal borehole thermal energy storage (BTES); strong PV/carport potential; grid constraints likely—apply early.
- Stevenage: industrial partners/process loads make heat recovery valuable; ambient loop could monetise simultaneous heating/cooling.
- White City: urban constraints favour ASHPs with acoustic mitigation, advanced energy recovery wheels, and rooftop PV field/carports.

8) Engagement and culture
- Lab user programs: sash campaigns, freezer management, shut‑off of bench equipment; publish lab league tables.
- O&M upskilling: lab HVAC/LEV competency for in‑house/FM teams; continuous commissioning.
- Stakeholder reporting: TCFD‑aligned risk disclosure; publish embodied carbon of MEP retrofits to evidence whole‑life trade‑offs.

This pathway recognises labs’ intrinsic high energy intensity and prioritises safe ventilation reduction, heat recovery, and electrification via campus ambient loops, underpinned by high‑quality renewable procurement and tenant alignment. It is deliverable within the stated capex envelope by phasing, with contingency for grid constraints and regulatory evolution, and aligns to SBTi and emerging UK operational performance standards.

Below is a pragmatic, PAS 2035–compliant, whole‑stock decarbonisation pathway for a 12,000‑home portfolio to achieve EPC C by 2030 and net zero by 2050, aligned to funding, risk, and delivery capacity. It assumes mixed-tenure social housing, typical constraints (planning, conservation, leaseholders), and leverages SHDF Wave 3 alongside HRA capex.

Portfolio snapshot and priorities
- Stock mix (approx.): 40% pre‑1919 solid-wall terraces; 35% 1960s system‑build towers/low-rise; 25% 1980s–2000s estate housing.
- Baseline performance: SAP 62 average (EPC D) with ~2,800 homes < EPC C.
- Funding: HRA ~£35m/yr ongoing; SHDF W3 award £18m over 3 years (assume ~£6m/yr 2026–2029, matched as required).
- Strategic principles:
  - PAS 2035: Whole-dwelling assessment, fabric-first, ventilation-first, least‑regrets, staged improvement pathways, and performance monitoring.
  - Risk-based sequencing: Address highest heat-loss archetypes and fuel poverty first; avoid stranded assets by ensuring measure compatibility with future heat decarbonisation.
  - Deliver through place-based “neighbourhood waves” to reduce cost, disruption, and maximise grid/heat network planning synergies.

Compliance framework under PAS 2035
- Retrofit Coordinator (RC) oversees each dwelling/phase; Retrofit Assessor (RA) produces RdSAP/occupancy assessment; Retrofit Designer (RD) creates improvement pathway; Retrofit Installer (RI) delivers to PAS 2030:2019/2023; Retrofit Evaluator (RE) verifies outcomes.
- Risk Pathways:
  - Path A (low): simpler cavity/loft/controls (mostly 1980s–2000s).
  - Path B (medium): mixed measures, some fabric and ventilation.
  - Path C (high): solid-wall pre‑1919; system-build towers/low-rise; external/internal wall insulation (EWI/IWI), MVHR, structural/fire interfaces, moisture risk. Most of your below‑C homes fall here.

Targets and key metrics
- EPC C by 2030 for all feasible homes; maintain average SAP/epc trajectory to avoid backsliding from fuel-switching or bill impacts.
- Heat demand intensity: move typical pre‑1919 to ≤90–100 kWh/m²/yr by 2030 where feasible; push ≤60–70 kWh/m²/yr before heat pump roll‑out post‑2030.
- Whole-life carbon: limit embodied carbon in major fabric elements; coordinate with planned maintenance cycles.

2026–2030: EPC C at scale, fabric-first and ventilation-first
Objectives
- Bring all feasible homes to EPC C, prioritising the 2,800 sub‑C units and worst-first estates.
- Prepare building envelopes for low‑temperature heat (post‑2030 heat pumps/heat networks).
- Establish data, governance, and supply chain for next phases.

Core interventions by archetype
1) Pre‑1919 solid-wall terraces (40%, high risk – Path C)
- Measures: External wall insulation (where street/heritage allows) with high-vapour-permeable systems; IWI in conservation/party-wall constrained homes; roof insulation top-up to 300 mm; suspended floor insulation/airtightness; high-performance doors/windows (A-rated or better, phased with cyclical works); whole-house ventilation strategy (MEV with boost or MVHR if airtightness ≤3–5 m³/hr·m²).
- Dependencies: Planning/listed building consent; moisture risk assessment; thermal bridging design; resident engagement for IWI; fire stopping around openings.
- Outcome: Typically lifts D/E to C/B and lowers heat demand to enable future heat pumps.

2) 1960s system-build towers/low-rise (35%, high risk – Path C)
- Measures: Whole-block façade remediation/EWI or overcladding integrated with fire safety compliance (A2-s1,d0 or better), compartmentation and structural checks; window replacement; communal ventilation upgrades; roof insulation; plant room optimisation; controls; hydraulic balancing; pipework insulation; lift/communal area asset coordination.
- Heat strategy: Pre-heat pump fabric/controls now; evaluate low‑temp communal heat pumps or heat network connection 2030–2040; for towers, prioritise central plant conversion over individual units.
- Critical interfaces: Fire Regulations (post‑Grenfell); BS 9414; leaseholder consultation; Section 20; planning.

3) 1980s–2000s estate housing (25%, Path A/B)
- Measures: Cavity wall extraction/refill where appropriate; loft top-ups; party-wall treatment; windows/doors at end-of-life; heating controls; low-cost airtightness works; ventilation upgrades (dMEV/MVHR where needed).
- Early heat pump pilots in homes already near C with good radiators/emitters; consider hybrid where fabric is borderline until deeper measures planned.

Cross-cutting enablers (2026–2030)
- Data and PAS processes:
  - Stock archetyping and dwelling-level PAS 2035 assessments; create improvement plans per archetype.
  - Digital twin/asset database linking SAP, metered energy (if available), fabric/MEP condition, fuel poverty flags.
- Procurement and delivery:
  - Long-term alliancing/frameworks with PAS 2030 certified SMEs and Tier 1 integrators; MMC for façade systems.
  - Place-based waves: deliver by estate/block/terrace runs.
- Resident engagement:
  - Clear sequencing, consent for IWI/EWI, decant strategies where unavoidable; usability training for controls and ventilation.
- Quality and performance:
  - Pre/post-works air tightness testing (sampled where appropriate); moisture monitoring for IWI cohorts; post-occupancy evaluation for a minimum 10% sample.
- Funding blend:
  - Deploy SHDF Wave 3 primarily on Path C homes (pre‑1919/system-build) with >50% fabric measures; match with HRA; align with ECO, GBIS where eligible; leverage VAT reliefs where applicable.

Indicative 2026–2030 outputs and spend
- Annual throughput: 1,800–2,200 homes/yr, frontloaded to sub‑C homes; by 2030, 100% at EPC C (allow for 3–5% technical exceptions with documented exemptions).
- Spend profile: £35m HRA/yr + ~£6m SHDF/yr for 3 years ≈ £41m/yr peak, tapering if SHDF ends; unit costs: £12–25k Path C; £3–8k Path A/B; block schemes capitalised over many units.

2030–2040: Heat decarbonisation at scale, deep fabric completions
Objectives
- Transition from gas to low‑carbon heat for the majority, prioritising buildings already fabric‑ready.
- Complete deeper fabric for hard‑to‑treat homes to achieve heat pump‑compatible loads and mitigate bill risk.
- Integrate local energy systems, grid capacity upgrades, and heat networks.

Strategic heat pathways by archetype
1) Towers and dense low-rise blocks
- Communal low‑temperature heat pumps (air‑to‑water or ambient loop GSHP), possibly hybridised with existing networks; thermal stores; smart controls; apartment-level HIUs.
- Where viable, connect to expanding 5th‑gen heat networks using WWHP or data centre waste heat.
- Sequencing: Fabric/ventilation and riser/fire compliance completed 2026–2030; plantroom conversion 2030–2036; in-flat emitter upgrades as needed.

2) Pre‑1919 terraces
- Individual air‑to‑water heat pumps after fabric brings peak heat loss to ≤50–70 W/m²; radiator upsizing; cylinder reintroduction for DHW; or micro‑heat networks for back‑to‑back terraces if streetscape limits ASHP siting.
- Consider hybrid HP as transitional only where planning/layout constraints persist, with sunset plan by 2040.

3) 1980s–2000s housing
- Scale individual ASHPs; some will already have been piloted; ensure EPC/SAP alignment with SCOP and low‑temp curves; PV + diverters and time-of-use tariffs.

Fabric and power system integration
- Finish remaining high-cost fabric (e.g., IWI where EWI not possible).
- Rooftop PV on estates and blocks with landlord supply optimisation; explore battery/shared storage at block level; EV readiness without compromising heat electrification capacity.
- DNO engagement: secure capacity, flexibility services, and phased connections; deploy demand response and heat pump control aggregation.

Quality, performance, and user outcomes
- Commissioning discipline: flow temps ≤45–50°C; weather compensation; room-by-room design.
- Post-occupancy support: helplines, seasonal visits; ensure bills do not rise—target running cost parity or better for vulnerable residents.
- Metered performance programmes for representative cohorts.

Funding and business case
- Blend HRA, SHDF successor/retrofit accelerators, ECO/GBIS, Ofgem innovation where applicable, Public Sector Decarbonisation for communal systems, and heat network funding for anchor loads.
- Whole-life cost view: coordinate end-of-life boiler replacement cycles to avoid stranded investment from 2030 onward.

2040–2050: Net zero completion, residuals, and optimisation
Objectives
- Eliminate residual fossil heat; address technical exceptions; deliver near‑zero operational emissions.
- Optimise systems, integrate storage/flex, and plan end-of-life replacements for heat pumps, façades, and MVHR.

Actions
- Replace any remaining gas assets; convert hybrids to all-electric; extend heat networks; targeted deep retrofits for the last 5–10% complex/heritage homes with bespoke solutions.
- Continuous optimisation: re-commission heat pumps after fabric changes; upgrade controls; expand PV and storage where economics allow; iterate with time-of-use and flexibility markets to lower bills and carbon.
- Embodied carbon and circularity: consider façade/plant renewals with low‑carbon materials; reuse strategies.

Sequencing and dependencies
- Technical:
  - Fabric before heat: achieve target heat loss and airtightness, confirm ventilation, then install low‑temp heat.
  - Fire and structure before façades; façade before windows if integrated system; internal works coordinated with rewires, kitchens/bathrooms where possible.
- Planning and consents:
  - Early engagement on EWI/IWI in conservation zones; ASHP siting; communal plant room alterations; heat network wayleaves/servitudes.
- Grid and networks:
  - Phased DNO applications 18–36 months ahead; coordinate EV infrastructure; secure heat network zones in Local Area Energy Plans.
- Resident and building management:
  - Leaseholder consultation and Section 20 for blocks; decant planning; vulnerable resident scheduling; clear aftercare.

Governance and delivery model
- Programme Office with:
  - Portfolio Retrofit Coordinator function and PAS compliance monitoring.
  - Archetype design guides and standard details library.
  - Tiered supply chain: façade specialists, MEP/communal heat, domestic heat pumps, ventilation, and QA testers.
  - KPIs: homes lifted to C; reduction in kWh/m²/yr; IAQ and condensation complaints; metered performance gap; resident satisfaction; fire safety compliance; spend vs. budget.
- Risk management: maintain risk register per archetype; insurance-backed guarantees; monitor mould/condensation risk post‑retrofit.

Regulatory and policy risks (and mitigations)
- PAS 2035 updates and transition to PAS 2035:2023/2030 installer standards changes: keep contracts flexible and suppliers accredited.
- Building Safety and Fire Regulations evolution: overcladding materials/fixings; require third-party certification and early fire engineer sign-off.
- EPC/SAP methodology changes (SAP 11/12, EPC reform): track changes that affect ratings of heat pumps and EWI; focus on measured performance and heat demand intensity, not EPC alone.
- Ecodesign/Boiler policy shifts and grid decarbonisation trajectory: avoid new gas assets post‑2030; design for 45–50°C systems to stay future-proof.
- Planning constraints for heritage/ASHP noise: pre-application engagement; batch planning; acoustic design.
- Funding volatility: diversify funding streams; keep shovel-ready packages; evidence outcomes to unlock future rounds.

Indicative milestones
- 2026: Programme office live; PAS processes embedded; first two place-based waves on site; 800–1,000 sub‑C homes underway.
- 2027–2029: 1,800–2,200 homes/yr; all feasible homes at EPC C by end-2029; communal block fabric complete on priority estates.
- 2030–2036: Convert priority blocks to communal heat pumps/heat networks; accelerate individual ASHP roll-out in terraces/estates; PV scaling.
- 2036–2040: Majority of stock off gas or on committed transition path; deep fabric residuals complete.
- 2040–2050: Final fossil removal, optimisation, replacements, and net zero verification.

Cost and affordability notes
- Achieving EPC C: average £8–15k/home blended; focus SHDF on Path C to keep average within HRA limits.
- Heat decarbonisation: additional £7–12k/home for individual ASHPs (post‑fabric), more for communal systems but with lifecycle savings.
- Manage lifetime cost by aligning with planned capital works (windows, roofs, MEP, fire) and avoiding double handling.

What to do next (first 6–12 months)
- Finalise archetype groupings and PAS 2035 preliminary designs; select pilot estates per archetype.
- Commission DNO capacity study and heat network zoning with LAEP alignment.
- Secure planning positions for EWI/IWI and standard ASHP details; establish conservation design codes.
- Execute procurement for multi-year, outcome-based contracts with PAS 2030 certified suppliers.
- Launch resident engagement and aftercare model; set up monitoring for IAQ and energy in pilot cohorts.
- Lock in SHDF Wave 3 delivery plan and monitoring/verification to de-risk drawdown.

This pathway meets PAS 2035 principles, delivers EPC C by 2030 for all feasible dwellings, and sets clear, sequenced foundations for cost-effective heat decarbonisation to achieve net zero by 2050.

Below is a pragmatic decarbonisation pathway for a UK BTR portfolio of 8,500 units (c.620,000 m2 GIA) on communal gas CHP/boilers with HIUs, targeting SBTi 1.5°C: -42% absolute Scope 1+2 by 2030 (vs 2022) and net zero by 2040. It assumes c.£45m/year capex and prioritises: (1) rapid Scope 2 cuts via electricity decarbonisation and building-side efficiency; (2) planned, scheme-by-scheme heat network conversion from gas to high-efficiency low‑carbon heat; (3) demand reduction to shrink future plant and operating costs; (4) commercial levers (green PPAs, tariffs) to de-risk timing.

Portfolio context and constraints
- Heat today: communal gas CHP/boilers feeding HIUs. CHP carbon advantage has largely eroded due to grid decarbonisation; many networks still bound by heat interface, hydraulic design (70/40–80/60°C), and metering.
- Fabric: new build 2018–2024, EPC B; good baseline but likely standard glazing, ventilation, and moderate airtightness.
- Tenant experience: BTR requires minimal disruption, stable bills, and service uptime; phasing and comms are critical.
- Capex: ~£45m/yr must cover surveys, pilots, fabric/controls, plant replacements, electrical upgrades, and contingencies.
- Carbon arithmetic: To achieve a 42% Scope 1+2 reduction by 2030, the lion’s share must come from (i) electrifying heat on at least a subset of schemes by 2030 and (ii) cutting electricity use and peak loads portfolio‑wide, with CHP run-hours sharply curtailed.

Key enablers and dependencies
- Electrical capacity: DNO capacity and onsite LV/HV constraints will gate heat pump rollouts; early applications and phased connections are essential.
- Flow temperature and ΔT: Many existing heat networks run 70–80°C. Successful heat pump conversion requires either:
  - Low-temperature networks (e.g., 55/25–45/25°C) through emitter upgrades, HIU setpoint changes, and network balancing; or
  - Cascaded or high‑temp heat pumps with careful COP impact and acoustic/space checks.
- Space/plant: Rooftop/plantroom for heat pumps, buffer and thermal stores; structural and acoustic surveys required, plus planning for external units.
- Metering and billing: Maintain or improve heat metering; re-commission after conversion.
- Tenant experience: Strong change management and staged outages; maintain resident trust.

Pathway overview
- 2026–2030: Stabilise and cut. Rapid Scope 2 actions, CHP de-optimisation, deep demand-side measures, and first-wave electrification (30–40% of heat load) focusing on “easy win” schemes.
- 2030–2035: Scale and standardise. Convert remaining mid-complexity schemes; expand low‑temp network retrofits; integrate thermal storage; prepare for or connect to 3rd‑party low‑carbon district heat where viable.
- 2035–2040: Finish and fine-tune. Complete last conversions (hard-to-treat), residual fabric upgrades, and optimise operations to achieve net zero (with minimal high-quality residuals if needed).

Detailed actions by phase

Phase 1: 2026–2030 (meet -42% Scope 1+2 by 2030)
Objectives
- Electrify a meaningful share of heat (target 30–40% portfolio heat load).
- Reduce electricity and heat demand 15–20% through controls and low‑intrusion efficiency.
- Eliminate CHP run-hours except for resilience/peak‑shaving where financially unavoidable.
- Lock in green electricity for residual Scope 2.

Workstreams
1) No-regrets portfolio measures (2026–2027 start; complete by 2029)
- BMS and controls optimisation across all 14 schemes: weather compensation, lower flow temps where feasible, tighter deadbands, night set-backs, HIU setpoint optimisation, pump VSD tuning, delta‑T improvement, fault detection and diagnostics (FDD).
- Heat loss reduction in distribution: re‑insulate mains/risers, fix bypasses, balance circuits; target ≥10% network loss reduction.
- Apartment-level measures: smart TRVs, resident app nudges, ventilation commissioning; offer fabric “light” measures at voids (sealant, trickle vents, door seals).
- Common areas: LED + controls; lift standby optimisation; car park ventilation demand control.
- PV on suitable roofs/facades; pair with heat pump plant where possible. Prioritise the 4–6 schemes with best solar yield. Consider PV carport canopies where roof area is constrained.
Impact: 8–12% portfolio energy reduction; improves business case for electrification.

2) CHP run strategy and gas reduction (from 2026)
- Curtail CHP baseloading; operate only for true peaking or where heat-led with demonstrable whole-system CO2e and cost benefit (likely minimal). Decommission or mothball where economics and carbon are negative.
- Replace failing gas boilers with modular interim high-efficiency units only if needed to bridge to heat pump conversion (avoid long-life locking).

3) First-wave heat pump conversions (2027–2030)
- Prioritise 4–6 schemes (30–40% of heat load) with:
  - Newer fabric and good ΔT (return ≤40°C achievable after balancing/HIU reset).
  - Sufficient plant space, crane access, and minimal planning risk.
  - Favorable DNO capacity or feasible private HV upgrade.
Technology options by scheme archetype:
- Low-temp network conversion (preferred): Central plantroom air-to-water or water-to-water heat pumps (if aquifer/WSHP or ambient loop feasible), deliver 50–60°C flow with network and HIU adjustments; add 1–2 MWh thermal stores for load shifting and demand response.
- Hybrid transition (temporary): Heat pumps sized to ~60–80% of peak with retained condensing boilers for very cold snaps; ratchet down boiler use annually as emitters/balancing improve.
- High-temp units only if necessary: Use 80°C-capable heat pumps or cascades where emitters cannot yet be replaced; expect COP penalty; plan staged move to lower temps by 2035.
Enablers:
- Early DNO applications (2026) and HV upgrades; consider private substation for larger sites.
- Acoustic mitigation and planning pre-apps; rooftop strengthening where needed.
- Migrate HIU control logic to suit lower flow temperatures (check DHW performance; consider point-of-use DHW boosters where peak DHW is critical).
- Thermal storage sized to shave electrified peak by 20–30%; explore flexibility revenues (DfD/DSR).
Carbon and cost:
- Expect 50–70% site CO2e reduction post-conversion (grid carbon trajectory dependent), with OPEX hedge via PPAs.
- Capex per scheme: £2–6m typical (size/complexity dependent). With £45m/yr, allocate ~£25–30m/yr to electrification, ~£10–12m to efficiency and PV, ~£3–5m to surveys, design, and DNO works.

4) Electricity decarbonisation and procurement (2026–2030)
- Enter sleeved or virtual PPA(s) covering 70–90% of portfolio electricity by 2027–2028; align term to 2035 with step-up volumes as heat electrifies.
- Residual supply on 100% REGO-backed tariff as interim, with a plan to tighten environmental integrity (hourly matching pilots at 1–2 flagship sites by 2029–2030).
- Submetering and M&V: Install MID-grade meters for plant and end-uses; follow IPMVP Option C portfolio with Option B at pilot sites.

5) Governance and resident strategy
- Resident bill protection: communicate running-cost expectations; maintain heat tariffs fair through conversion; bill smoothing during transition.
- Outage planning: plant-by-plant changeover scheduled shoulder seasons; contingency temporary boilers.
- Data and reporting: quarterly carbon/energy dashboards to track SBTi progress.

Phase 1 outcomes by 2030
- 30–40% of portfolio heat converted to heat pumps/hybrids; CHP largely offline.
- 15–20% demand reduction from controls/fabric-light; PV on 25–35% of roof area.
- PPA-backed electricity for Scope 2; portfolio Scope 1 significantly reduced.
- Achieve ≥42% absolute Scope 1+2 reduction vs 2022 with headroom for grid variability.

Phase 2: 2030–2035 (scale to majority electrification)
Objectives
- Convert an additional 40–50% of heat load to low‑carbon.
- Transition networks to lower temperatures portfolio-wide, reducing heat pump lift and OPEX.
- Integrate larger thermal stores and flexibility to manage grid constraints and tariffs.
- Leverage external low‑carbon district heat where credible.

Workstreams
1) Second-wave conversions (2030–2034)
- Tackle medium-complexity schemes: limited space, trickier hydraulics, or moderate planning constraints.
- Increase share of water-source or ambient loop where feasible (surface water, aquifers, sewer heat, data centre waste heat). Conduct feasibility studies 2029–2030.
- Standardise plant designs and controls architectures to drive down unit capex and commissioning time.

2) Network temperature downgrades and emitters
- Systematically reduce flow temps: target 55/25°C or lower where achievable.
- Replace undersized emitters in common areas; selectively upgrade apartment emitters at voids/refurbs; fit low-temp DHW boosters if needed for Legionella compliance on lower primary flow.
- Widespread rebalance and delta‑T optimisation; target 10–15°C return temperature drops vs current.

3) Storage and flexibility
- Add larger stratified thermal stores (2–6 MWh) to shift to off-peak/renewable-heavy hours.
- Enrol in DSO flexibility markets and capacity services where viable; adopt dynamic tariffs; implement automated control to optimise against carbon intensity signals.

4) External heat networks
- For sites near credible, low‑carbon district heat (e.g., >80% non‑fossil primary), compare LCOH and carbon to onsite heat pumps. Negotiate connection windows 2031–2034, ensuring tariff transparency and exit provisions.

5) Procurement evolution
- Expand or renew PPA volumes to match higher electrical load; explore 24/7 carbon-matched supply pilots on 1–2 large schemes by 2033–2035.
- Continue PV and consider BESS where grid export constraints exist and heat pump cycling can benefit.

Phase 2 outcomes by 2035
- 70–85% of portfolio heat decarbonised (onsite HP or verified low‑carbon district heat).
- Network temperatures lowered; COPs materially improved; OPEX stabilised.
- Scope 1 largely eliminated except for residual backup boilers and last schemes awaiting conversion.
- On track for net zero 2040 with limited residual emissions.

Phase 3: 2035–2040 (complete and optimise to net zero)
Objectives
- Convert final hard-to-treat schemes and eliminate routine fossil backup use.
- Close remaining performance gaps; enhance monitoring, maintenance, and optimisation.
- Address any residual emissions with high-quality neutralisation only after deep reductions.

Workstreams
1) Final conversions and decommissioning (2035–2038)
- For schemes with severe constraints, deploy:
  - Cascaded or high-temp heat pumps paired with targeted emitter upgrades to enable moderate temp drops.
  - Hybrid setups with minimal boiler runtime; progressively remove gas by 2038–2040.
- Decommission CHPs; repurpose space and connections.

2) Deep fabric at end-of-life
- Align fabric upgrades with lifecycle events (window replacements, roof/façade works) to lift thermal performance and enable lower flow temperatures sustainably.
- Improve airtightness and MVHR where appropriate to stabilise comfort and bills.

3) 24/7 clean electricity
- Extend PPAs and add storage to approach hourly matching at flagship schemes; evaluate on-site/off-site wind or solar partnerships.

4) Net zero verification
- Implement third-party assurance of Scope 1+2; residual emissions (e.g., emergency generator testing, fugitive refrigerants) neutralised with durable, high-quality removals.

Key risks, mitigations, and regulatory watchpoints
- Grid capacity and connection delays
  - Risk: DNO timelines slip; constraint charges.
  - Mitigation: Apply early; stage loads; use thermal storage, smart controls, and temporary hybrids; consider private wire or on-site generation.
- Planning and acoustic constraints for external units
  - Mitigation: Early acoustic design, placement, screens, vibration isolation; engage planners with visuals and noise studies.
- Legionella/DHW at lower temps
  - Mitigation: HIU/DHW design review; point-of-use electric boosters; periodic pasteurisation; robust H&S regime.
- EPC/MES compliance
  - EPC methodology is evolving towards SAP 11; electrification should improve ratings over gas CHP as grid carbon falls. Monitor Future Homes/Buildings Standards and MEES tightening for non-domestic areas.
- Heat network regulation
  - OFGEM regulation of heat networks from 2025–2026: consumer protection, price transparency, service standards; ensure metering accuracy, fair tariffs, and outage management.
- Boiler/CHP policy trajectory
  - Anticipate diminishing support for CHP as the grid decarbonises; avoid reinvestment in CHP. Prepare for potential gas connection constraints post-2035.
- Electricity market reform and locational pricing
  - Mitigation: PPAs with flexible baseload + shape; diversify geographies; embed flexibility in plant controls.
- Refrigerant transition
  - F‑gas phase-down: specify low‑GWP refrigerants (e.g., R-1234ze(E), R-290) and leak detection; plan mitigations for hydrocarbon safety.
- Embodied carbon and circularity
  - Track embodied carbon of plant replacements; prioritise refurbishment of existing assets where possible; recycle CHP assets responsibly.

High-level capital allocation (indicative)
- 2026–2030: £45m/yr
  - 55–65% heat pump conversions and enabling works
  - 20–25% efficiency (controls, rebalancing, insulation, HIU optimisation), metering, analytics
  - 10–15% PV and selective storage
  - 5–10% surveys, DNO, planning, contingencies
- 2030–2035: £45m/yr
  - 65–75% conversions and emitter/network temp works
  - 10–15% storage/flexibility
  - 10–15% PV/BESS expansion
  - 5–10% fabric at lifecycle touchpoints
- 2035–2040: £35–45m/yr (may taper as portfolio completes)
  - 60–70% final conversions and decommissioning
  - 10–15% deep fabric at lifecycle events
  - 10–15% 24/7 clean power solutions and storage
  - 5–10% optimisation, commissioning, verification

Measurement and SBTi alignment
- Base year: 2022. Set annual interim targets and publish a glidepath to 2030.
- Metering and M&V: granular submetering at each plant; IPMVP-compliant savings verification; track heat pump SPF/SCOP seasonally.
- Accounting: Use market-based Scope 2 with transparent PPA quality; also report location-based to demonstrate real-world progress.
- Governance: Quarterly energy/carbon reviews; tie asset manager incentives to kWh/m2 and kgCO2e targets; resident satisfaction tracked during transitions.

What success looks like
- By 2030: ≥42% absolute Scope 1+2 reduction; 30–40% of heat electrified; CHP largely retired; strong data backbone.
- By 2035: 70–85% of heat low‑carbon; network temps reduced; robust PPAs; stable or lower resident energy bills versus 2024 baseline (normalized).
- By 2040: All schemes on heat pumps or verified low‑carbon district heat; fossil backup eliminated; net zero Scope 1+2 with negligible residuals.

Next 6–9 months (immediate actions)
- Portfolio heat decarb roadmap at Level 2 design per scheme; rank by readiness and carbon/cost impact.
- DNO capacity applications and HV strategy for top 6 schemes.
- Controls re-commissioning across all schemes; initiate metering upgrades.
- PPA procurement RFP, aligned with staged electrification.
- Planning and acoustic pre-apps for first-wave conversions.
- Resident engagement plan and tariffs review to ensure fair, transparent heat pricing through transition.

This staged plan confronts the embedded gas heat network challenge head-on, uses capex efficiently, protects resident experience, and credibly achieves the investor’s SBTi 1.5°C pathway to 2030 and net zero by 2040.

Below is a practical decarbonisation pathway for the PBSA portfolio that fits the spend envelope (~£12m/year), aligns to SBTi (50% by 2030; net zero by 2038), and manages regulatory and delivery risks. It recognises seasonal occupancy (term time vs summer lets), the mixed asset typologies, and PRS MEES exposure.

1) Strategic framing and governance (0–6 months)
- Establish PBSA Energy & Carbon Programme Board with estates, finance, housing, procurement, IT, and student reps. Tie decisions to the ring‑fenced PBSA income and a multi‑year investment plan.
- Create an asset-level carbon and cost model:
  - Metering and sub‑metering baseline by hall and end-use (space heat, DHW, lighting, small power) with half‑hourly data.
  - Normalise against degree days and occupancy (term vs vacation) to separate building fabric/plant performance from load variation.
  - Attribute scope 1 vs 2 per hall to pinpoint gas vs electric transition opportunities and quantify grid-intensity trajectories.
- Lock an internal carbon price (e.g., £100/tCO2e escalating to £200 by 2030) within the business case template so marginal abatement cost guides prioritisation alongside NPV and student experience.
- Develop a heat decarbonisation roadmap integrated with planned lifecycle replacements to minimise throwaway capex.

2) Compliance context: MEES and PRS applicability
- Determine PRS status: If any PBSA is let on Assured Shorthold Tenancies or otherwise falls into PRS, MEES applies. Purpose-built halls often sit outside PRS where lettings are licences rather than ASTs, but mixed models/third‑party nominations can trigger PRS. Commission legal review hall-by-hall.
- MEES trajectory and risk:
  - Current: E minimum for leases; government consulted on C by 2028 for non‑domestic and EPC C for domestic PRS—policy is fluid, but investors and lenders expect uplift.
  - EPC caveats: EPCs poorly reflect real heat decarb (e.g., penalising electric heat on assumed tariffs). Still, EPC D average is a reputational/regulatory risk. Target EPC B portfolio average by 2030 to keep ahead of MEES tightening and borrowing covenants.
- Student visa and HMO/local licensing: Ensure interventions (e.g., window replacement, ventilation) maintain compliance with space standards, fire safety (BS 9991/BS 8629 where relevant), overheating (BB101/CIBSE TM59), and acoustic regs.

3) Decarbonisation hierarchy and seasonal occupancy strategy
- Reduce demand first (fabric/controls), then decarbonise heat, then optimise operations and engage occupants.
- Seasonal occupancy:
  - Use low-occupancy summer periods for intrusive works (windows, façades, risers, plant rooms) and term-time for plant commissioning, controls optimisation and room-level measures requiring short access.
  - Implement flexible zoning, set-back strategies, and vacancy detection to exploit shoulder seasons. Vacation shutdown protocols for blocks not in use.
  - Expand summer conferencing selectively in buildings already electrified/efficient to avoid locking in gas runtime.

4) Interventions by archetype with phasing and budget
Assumptions: £12m/year ring‑fenced; allow 10–15% inflation/contingency; pursue Salix/PSDS or OfS/UKIB matches where eligible to stretch spend; sequence to hit 50% Scope 1+2 by 2030.

A) 1960s towers (solid concrete, single glazing, electric storage heating)
- Issues: Very poor fabric, direct electric storage heat (high Scope 2, high bills, comfort issues), single glazing causing heat loss/overheating.
- Measures (priority 1: 2026–2030):
  - Windows: Replace single glazing with high‑performance double/triple low‑E, thermally broken frames; address air‑tightness systemically (target q50 ≤5 m³/h·m²). Include trickle or MVHR compatibility.
  - External wall insulation (EWI) or over‑cladding with non‑combustible systems; coordinate with fire safety remediation; improve thermal bridges at slabs.
  - Whole‑building ventilation upgrade: Balanced MVHR where feasible; otherwise demand-controlled MEV with local heat recovery in wet cores; install CO2 sensors for control.
  - Electrification: Replace storage heaters with variable-refrigerant-flow (VRF/VRV) or central air-to-water heat pumps with low‑temp emitters; consider thermal buffer tanks. If roof area suits, split DX heat pumps per vertical zone.
  - Hot water: Central high‑temp heat pumps (e.g., CO2) with stratified cylinders; restrict electric immersion to sterilisation backup.
  - Controls: Room thermostats with occupancy sensing; BMS integration; wireless where fabric constraints exist.
  - Onsite PV: Maximise roofs/facades; pair with heat pump daytime operation/thermal storage to flatten demand.
- Outcomes: 35–55% site energy reduction from fabric/controls; >70% carbon cut vs storage heating once grid decarbonisation is factored. EPC uplift typically to B/C.
- Budget guide: £350–600/m² for deep retrofit packages; prioritise best candidates (structural integrity, façade access) first. Allocate ~£6–7m/yr for 3–4 years to retrofit 2–3 towers per year.

B) 1990s en‑suite cluster flats (gas boilers, cavity wall)
- Issues: Gas heating/DHW, moderate fabric, aging boilers; often decent cavities but thermal bridging and ventilation gaps.
- Measures (priority 1–2: 2026–2032):
  - Fabric: Cavity wall insulation top‑ups/reinstatement; loft/roof insulation where accessible; address airtightness at service penetrations; replace older double glazing where failed.
  - Heating conversion: Two pathways by block:
    - Central plant blocks: Convert to central low‑temp distribution with air-to-water heat pumps in plant room or courtyard, upgrade emitters to LTHW radiators/fan coils; add thermal storage.
    - Decentralised: Replace flat boilers with monobloc air-to-water or hybrid heat pumps; or move to VRF with hydronic DHW.
  - DHW: Central CO2 heat pumps with preheat and point‑of‑use boosters for pasteurisation; improve recirc controls and pipe insulation.
  - Smart zoning and weather compensation; TRVs to eTRVs; BMS expansion.
  - PV and limited battery where export constrained.
- Outcomes: 40–60% gas reduction immediately; 60–80% Scope 1 reduction by 2030 if heat pumps adopted; EPC uplift to B/C.
- Budget guide: £120–250/m² for fabric/controls; £2,000–4,000/room for heat pump conversion depending on central vs decentralised. Allocate ~£3–4m/yr.

C) 2015+ studios (communal gas heating, EPC B)
- Issues: Good fabric and EPC; remaining Scope 1 from communal gas boilers; opportunity for low‑disruption plant swaps and optimisation.
- Measures (priority 2: 2028–2032, or earlier at end‑of‑life):
  - Plant-room swap to high‑efficiency heat pumps sized for base load with gas peak/top‑up initially if needed; low‑temp distribution check.
  - DHW: Heat pump with high‑temp CO2 for cylinders; demand‑driven recirculation.
  - Advanced controls, weather compensation, dynamic tariffs integration; continuous commissioning.
- Outcomes: Rapid Scope 1 reduction with limited capex; EPC to A/B.
- Budget guide: £1,500–3,000/bed for plant conversion; allocate ~£1–2m/yr around boiler EoL.

Cross-portfolio quick wins (2026–2028)
- LED and controls completion: Residual stairwells, exteriors, plant rooms; adaptive lighting with occupancy.
- BMS analytics and fault detection (FDD); submetering expansion to room and riser levels where practical.
- Water efficiency (low‑flow, leak detection) to reduce DHW loads.
- ICT: Smart plug load management; default low-power settings on supplied devices.
- Refrigerants: Specify low-GWP refrigerants for heat pumps/VRF and a leak detection/maintenance regime.

5) Phasing and targets
- 2026: Complete metering/BMS/FDD baseline; legal MEES review; lock procurement frameworks; pilot one tower deep retrofit and one 1990s block heat pump/DHW conversion; PV phase 1.
- 2027–2029: Roll out towers (2–3/year) and 1990s blocks (3–5/year). Convert 2–3 communal plant rooms in 2015+ stock as boilers hit EoL. Achieve EPC C or better for 80% of beds by 2029.
- 2030 milestone: 50% Scope 1+2 reduction from PBSA vs baseline; portfolio EPC average B/C; demand reduction of 25–30% kWh/m² across retrofitted assets.
- 2031–2034: Complete remaining 1990s stock conversions; finish towers; all communal plants heat pump-based with limited or no gas backup; PV build-out complete; consider campus heat networks if available.
- 2035–2038: Residual elimination: phase out remaining gas peaks; top up fabric where needed; procure 100% additionality-backed renewable electricity (PPAs); address any outliers for net-zero operational carbon.

6) Occupancy, wellbeing, and student experience
- Comfort and health: Design for TM59 overheating compliance (especially post‑insulation/window upgrades); include shading and solar control glass. Maintain acoustic performance.
- Access and decant: Use rolling floor closures in vacation; if full decant needed for towers, align with exam and move‑out calendars and offer rent rebates or alternative halls.
- Behavioural programmes: Real-time room energy dashboards; competitions by floor; default 19–20°C setpoints with opt‑out; opt‑in vacation shutdown.
- Accessibility: Avoid creating temperature disparities; provide clear instructions for new controls.

7) Energy procurement and flexibility
- Electricity: Move towards long-term renewable PPAs aligned with electrification curve; hedge volumes gradually as heat pumps come online.
- Demand flexibility: Enrol buildings with heat pumps and thermal storage into DSR; pre‑heat/pre‑cool strategies during low-carbon/low-cost periods; export PV where viable or store thermally.
- EV and logistics: If EV charging for staff/visitors, use smart charging; ensure it doesn’t peak‑clash with heat pumps.

8) Financials and funding
- Use the £12m/year ring‑fence as the base. Sequence high-IRR towers first (because storage heat to heat pumps + fabric yields large carbon and bill cuts).
- Seek co‑funding: Salix PSDS (when open), local authority grants for heat networks if relevant, innovation pilots (OfS, Innovate UK).
- Procurement: Establish heat pump and façade frameworks; performance‑based contracts with guaranteed kWh/m² reductions; consider EPC (Energy Performance Contract) for a subset.

9) Measurement, verification, and reporting
- Adopt IPMVP Option C at building level with normalisation to occupancy and weather; publish annual hall scorecards.
- Align reporting to SBTi and HE sector frameworks (EAUC/BUFDG), and disclose EPC progression.

10) Key dependencies and risks
- Grid capacity: Early DNO engagement; heat pump electrification may need LV/HV upgrades. Mitigations: phasing, on-site PV, thermal/electrical storage, transformer upgrades included in scope.
- Planning/listed status: Some towers may face façade constraints; use secondary glazing and internal insulation where external is restricted; ensure fire strategy compliance for any cladding.
- MEES/regulatory uncertainty: Even if MEES stalls, lenders and students expect EPC B. Maintain a “no‑regrets” list (fabric, controls, metering, PV) and avoid new gas plant unless genuinely transitional.
- Supply chain: Secure heat pump and façade capacity via frameworks; standardise designs by archetype; include refrigerant management and commissioning quality plans.
- Cost inflation: Hold contingencies; batch‑procure windows and heat pumps; consider offsite façade panels.
- Performance gap: Commissioning agent and soft‑landings through the first heating season; tie contractor payment to in‑use performance.
- Legionella and DHW temperatures: Use high‑temp heat pumps or periodic pasteurisation strategies; verify recirc balance.
- Fire safety: Non‑combustible insulation and cladding; review compartmentation after M&E penetrations; coordinate with fire strategy updates.
- Overheating: Post‑retrofit risk increases; incorporate shading and ventilation strategy; monitor in first summer.

11) Indicative carbon savings contribution to 2030 target
- Towers deep retrofit + electrification (covering ~1,800–2,200 beds): 1,600–2,100 tCO2e/yr
- 1990s blocks fabric + partial/complete electrification (~3,000–3,500 beds): 1,600–2,000 tCO2e/yr
- 2015+ plant swaps and optimisation (~1,000–1,500 beds): 400–600 tCO2e/yr
- PV + controls + behavioural + FDD: 300–500 tCO2e/yr
- Total indicative: 3,900–5,200 tCO2e/yr, sufficient to deliver the 50% reduction by 2030 from 5,200 tCO2e baseline, with headroom for grid-intensity uncertainty.

12) Next steps (practical 90‑day plan)
- Weeks 1–4: Commission legal MEES review; appoint M&V lead; DNO capacity enquiry; thermal modeling for one tower and one 1990s block; launch sub‑metering spec.
- Weeks 5–8: RIBA 2–3 designs for pilot tower retrofit and 1990s block heat pump/DHW; planning pre‑app; procurement strategy and frameworks.
- Weeks 9–12: Finalise business cases with carbon price; student comms plan; book summer works windows; order long‑lead items (windows, heat pumps); apply for any open grants.

This pathway balances early, high-impact retrofits with scalable plant conversions, keeps EPC and MEES risks under control, respects seasonal operations, and delivers the SBTi-aligned reductions within the funding constraint.

Below is a practical PAS 2035-compliant pathway tailored to your stock profile, funding envelope and targets, and the particular risks of non‑traditional construction. It is structured around roles and stages in PAS 2035, the technical interventions by archetype, delivery sequencing and dependencies, governance/assurance, and regulatory risks.

1) Strategic framing and targets
- Objectives: Lift all homes to EPC C by 2030; align decarbonisation trajectory to net zero by 2050. Reduce heat demand first, then decarbonise heat, with health and safety/non‑disrepair as a non-negotiable prerequisite at each step.
- Scale: c.3,800 homes below C are priority for SHDF Wave 3+ and internal capex. Maintain uplift momentum for the remainder to avoid 2030 cliff-edge.
- Funding: £90m/yr major works plus £32m SHDF Wave 3. Blend with ECO4/GBIS, Boiler Upgrade Scheme (BUS) for off-gas archetypes, and potential LAEP/DSO flexibility revenues where heat pumps/thermal stores deployed at scale.

2) PAS 2035 governance, roles and process
- Retrofit Strategy and Client Brief (PAS 2035: Plan)
  - Establish a Retrofit Programme Board (director-level sponsor; asset, sustainability, H&S, finance, procurement). Approve archetype playbooks, risk appetite, and KPI suite.
  - Confirm PAS 2035 compliance scope: all sub‑C homes and any homes receiving energy efficiency measures, plus a risk-based approach for C-rated homes that will receive heating system changes.
- Roles
  - Retrofit Coordinator (RC, Level appropriate to risk): end-to-end case management, lodge to TrustMark, oversee design, QA, handover and POE.
  - Retrofit Assessor: RdSAP/SAP, condition survey, ventilation assessment, significance of moisture risks.
  - Retrofit Designer: qualified to manage medium/high moisture risk (especially solid-wall and non-trad).
  - Retrofit Evaluator: POE on representative samples; thermal imaging, airtightness tests where relevant.
- Risk pathways (PAS 2035)
  - Path A (low risk): most post‑1980 cavity-wall estate properties with conventional measures.
  - Path B (medium risk): pre‑1919 solid-wall terraces without atypical defects; some No-Fines where prior evidence exists.
  - Path C (high risk): all non‑traditional PRC/reinforced concrete systems (Cornish Unit, Reema), any known structural, chloride/carbonation, or significant moisture risks; conservation/complex terraces.
- Process checkpoints
  - Whole-dwelling assessments including: damp/mould, ventilation (Part F), fire safety, structural movement, services, occupant needs, fuel poverty/tenure.
  - Medium-Term Improvement Plan (MTIP) per dwelling (20–30 year), aligned to stock investment plans and net-zero pathway.
  - Design sign-off with hygrothermal modelling (WUFI/HEAT2 as required) for EWI/IWI on solid and non‑trad walls; condensation risk analysis; fixings/bridging details; fire strategy for any façade works.
  - Pre-installation ventilation upgrades if airtightness measures are planned (PAS 2035 requires).
  - Commissioning, handover (user guidance), and evaluation with sampling strategy (e.g., 10% POE for Path B, 20% for Path C).
  - TrustMark lodgement and data feedback loop into your asset system.

3) Archetype-specific strategies and measures
A) Post-1980 estate housing (c.60%; mostly EPC C; gas)
- Aim: Secure C across any laggards; prepare for heat decarbonisation and demand flexibility.
- Likely Path: A (low risk), batch delivery by estate.
- Measures
