  - Fabric first top-ups: cavity wall insulation QA/defect rectification; loft insulation to 300 mm; insulated hatches; party-wall insulation where cost-effective; replacement of failed DGUs to modern low-e; targeted airtightness (service penetrations) with matching ventilation upgrades.
  - Controls: smart TRVs, weather/compensation control, time/temperature zoning; ensure Boiler Plus compliance now, heat-pump ready later.
  - Heating roadmap: for properties with lifecycle boiler replacements within 5–10 years, specify heat-pump-ready emitters (oversize radiators/pipework) during cyclical works. Pilot low-temperature operation on condensing boilers to de-risk future heat pump installs.
  - PV and demand flexibility: estate-scale PV where roof orientation allows; prepare for DSR/ToU tariffs with smart meters and controls; consider shared inverters or roof lease models.
- Dependencies: grid capacity checks at feeder level if moving to heat pumps post-2030; coordination with roof replacement cycles.
- Risks: Over-insulation of cavities with existing defects; ensure surveillance borescope/IR surveys and CWI extraction where saturated.

B) Pre-1919 solid-wall terraces (c.25%; EPC E–F)
- Aim: Lift to C by 2030 with moisture-safe fabric measures; avoid unintended condensation/mould; set up for low-temperature heat.
- Likely Path: B/C (medium to high risk).
- Measures
  - Fabric
    - External Wall Insulation (EWI) as default for workable elevations: high-vapour-permeable systems with carefully designed window reveals, cills, eaves and DPC junctions; manage thermal bridges at party wall/exposed gables.
    - Internal Wall Insulation (IWI) only where façades are constrained: capillary-active systems (calcium silicate/aerogel in tight spaces) with robust vapour control, pre-works damp remediation, and services re-routing. Mandatory hygrothermal modelling and moisture monitoring.
    - Floor insulation (suspended timber): breathable insulation beneath with ventilation maintained; remediate rot; install airtightness membranes at floor edges.
    - Loft/roof: to 300 mm; insulate/airtight at attic hatches; consider rafter-level insulation on reroof cycles.
    - Airtightness package: chimney/fireplace strategies; draught-proofing; then guarantee compliant ventilation.
  - Ventilation
    - Upgrade to continuous MEV or dMEV with humidity control; consider MVHR only post-airtightness testing (<3–5 m³/h·m² @50Pa) and where maintenance can be supported.
  - Heating
    - For on-gas: retain boilers short-term but design for 45–50°C flow; radiator upsizing now to be heat-pump ready.
    - Off-gas or high fuel poverty clusters: target heat pumps under BUS/SHDF with prior fabric upgrades.
  - Renewable options: PV where roof orientation/heritage allows; solar thermal rarely cost-effective vs PV + HP.
- Dependencies: planning/heritage approvals; party wall agreements; street-facing EWI aesthetics; cavity-like party wall thermal bypass treatments.
- Risks: Moisture load increase with IWI; interstitial condensation; cold bridging at joist ends; ensure joist end assessments and detail drawings. Fire spread at façades: select A2-s1,d0 or per fire engineer advice; ensure cavity barriers. Resident disruption management essential.

C) Non-traditional construction (c.15%; Cornish Unit, Wimpey No-Fines, Reema, others)
- Aim: Achieve C with structurally and hygrothermally safe solutions, with clear structural remediation sequencing.
- Likely Path: C (high risk), case-by-case with system-specific playbooks.
- Sub-archetype notes
  - Cornish Unit (Type 1/2 PRC) and Reema (hollow panel)
    - Structural: Many are designated defective under the Housing Defects Act; confirm if previously repaired (licensed schemes). Undertake intrusive surveys: carbonation depth, chloride content, PRC stanchions condition, wall ties/fixings strategy.
    - Remediation: Where unrepaired or failing, consider licensed PRC repair (rebuild envelope) before energy measures. In some cases, full redevelopment/replacement may be better value than deep retrofit—include NPV and liability risk analysis in MTIP.
    - Thermal strategy: After structural remediation, EWI with mechanically appropriate fixings to new leaf; address balcony/column bridges; ensure fire compliance and cavity barriers.
  - Wimpey No-Fines
    - Hygrothermal: Monolithic no-fines concrete has high vapour permeability but low capillarity; EWI works well if detailed to avoid trapped moisture and if fixings account for pull-out in coarse aggregate mix; pre-works moisture and IR scans.
    - Airtightness can be poor at junctions; address soffit/wall junctions and penetrations; upgrade ventilation.
  - Other steel frame or timber frame systems
    - Condensation risk at sheathing layers; avoid IWI unless modelled; prefer EWI with breathable render; check sheathing integrity and DPC/DPM continuity.
- Common measures
  - Roof insulation and airtightness; replacement of failing windows/doors with suitable cavity closers/air seals.
  - Ventilation upgrades mandatory before or alongside airtightness.
- Dependencies: Structural certification, warranties, planning for façade treatments, resident decanting for intrusive works.
- Risks: Fixing failure on EWI; fire performance; latent defects liability; insurer and lender acceptance—retain full design and QA pack.

4) Programme phasing and delivery model (to 2030 and beyond)
- 2024–2026: Mobilise and de-risk
  - Data enhancement: Stock segmentation to archetype level; EPC/SAP gap-filling; moisture/damp survey programme for pre‑1919 and non‑trad; pilot airtightness testing.
  - Early wins: Fabric-plus-heating-controls on post‑1980 C‑minus homes to secure C quickly. Tackle worst E/F fuel poverty homes with SHDF Wave 3.
  - Pathfinder projects: 200–400 homes each for solid-wall EWI/IWI and for each key non‑trad type to prove details, QS rates, and POE results.
  - Procurement: Set up PAS 2035-compliant frameworks/lots by archetype; outcome-based specs (kWh/m² targets, airtightness, IAQ).
- 2026–2029: Scale with standardisation
  - Roll out estate-by-estate packages for post‑1980 homes; batch procurement for EWI on terraces and No-Fines; expand heat pump clusters where fabric is ready and grid allows.
  - Integrate with cyclical works: align roof/window/boiler cycles to avoid rework; implement emitter upsizing during heating replacements.
  - Digital twin/asset data: capture measure-level data, U-values, airtightness, ventilation type; link to compliance and future heat transition planning.
- 2029–2030: EPC C assurance
  - Sweep-up interventions for stragglers; address hard cases with targeted extra measures (e.g., secondary glazing, advanced IWI).
  - Independent audit sampling, POE, IAQ checks, and SAP re-assessments to confirm C achievement and SHDF claims.
- 2030–2040: Heat decarbonisation ramp
  - Transition zones: off-gas first, then gas grid areas as network capacity and costs improve.
  - Pilot networked solutions: shared ground arrays on estates; ambient loop with HIUs in blocks.
  - Flexibility: deploy thermal storage, smart controls, and tariffs to cut peak loads; explore RAB/ESCO models for shared infrastructure.

5) Costing, funding and prioritisation
- Triage scoring
  - Energy: EPC band, heat demand (kWh/m²), tenure and fuel poverty.
  - Deliverability: archetype readiness, planning risk, decant need.
  - Co-benefits: damp/mould risk, HHSRS hazards, health outcomes, regeneration alignment.
- Funding stack
  - SHDF Wave 3 for E/F/G to C, particularly solid-wall and non‑trad after fabric-first measures.
  - ECO4/GBIS for insulation and heating controls in eligible homes.
  - BUS for heat pumps in off-gas or where gas boilers end-of-life and fabric ready.
  - LAEP/networks for connection to low-carbon heat zones if available.
- Benchmark costs (indicative, vary by scale/market)
  - Post‑1980 C-ups: £2–6k/home.
  - Solid-wall EWI packages: £18–28k/home; IWI: £12–22k/home but higher risk.
  - Non-trad structural + EWI: highly variable, £25–60k/home; full PRC remediation can exceed this—test against redevelopment.

6) Quality assurance, performance and resident outcomes
- Technical QA
  - Designs: junction details library; hygrothermal modelling records; fire strategy statements for façades.
  - Site QA: photographic evidence, pull-out tests for fixings, airtightness tests on sample basis, ventilation commissioning certificates, smoke tests, thermal imaging post-works in heating season.
  - POE: temperature/RH/CO2 loggers in sample homes; energy use normalised for weather; mould reinspection at 3, 12 months.
- Resident engagement
  - Early consent and expectations, especially for IWI/EWI and decants.
  - Simple user guides; in-home demos on ventilation systems and controls; post-install support line.
  - Vulnerability protocols to manage disruption and ensure safe internal conditions during works.

7) Data, compliance and reporting
- TrustMark and PAS 2035 lodgements for all funded measures; maintain a golden thread of design, installation, and evaluation records.
- Update SAP/SBtD data after works; store measure meta-data (manufacturer, thickness, location).
- ESG/bond reporting: annual disclosure of homes uplifted to C+, modelled and actual carbon reductions, IAQ/damp outcomes, and spend against sustainability-linked KPIs.
- Net-zero pathway model: maintain stock-level heat demand and system mix forecast; scenario test gas grid decommissioning, hydrogen unlikely scenarios, and electricity price trajectories.

8) Key dependencies and enablers
- Planning and heritage: early engagement for solid-wall streets; develop standard façade palettes and details; party wall processes.
- Supply chain capacity: invest in installer training for high-risk IWI/EWI and non‑trad systems; partner with system manufacturers for warranties and detail support.
- Grid capacity: DNO engagement for cluster heat pump plans; pursue timed connections and flexibility assets to defer reinforcement.
- Procurement: outcome-based, PAS 2035-compliant, with KPIs on defects, IAQ, and resident satisfaction; include social value.

9) Regulatory and policy risks, with mitigations
- PAS 2035/TrustMark changes: Version updates may tighten requirements on ventilation and evaluation. Mitigation: keep framework lots flexible; maintain RC competency matrix and CPD.
- Building Regulations
  - Part L uplift implications for backstop U-values; Mitigate by designing to current/new backstops and documenting exemptions where not technically feasible.
  - Part F (ventilation): risk of condensation/mould claims if not met. Mitigate via mandatory ventilation upgrades and commissioning.
  - Part B (fire safety): façade combustibility and cavity barriers; mitigate with A2-s1,d0+ systems, fire engineer sign-off, especially above 11 m and in blocks.
- Fuel poverty and mould/damp regulation: strengthened obligations post-HHSRS review. Mitigate by prioritising damp/mould risk homes and evidencing IAQ improvements.
- EPC/SAP methodology shifts (SAP 11): changes to ratings may reclassify bands. Mitigate by targeting real heat demand (kWh/m²) outcomes and embedding headroom above current C thresholds.
- Funding compliance risk (SHDF/ECO/BUS): evidence and M&V requirements; Mitigate with robust data capture and audit trails.
- Net-zero policy volatility (hydrogen for heat unlikely but uncertain): avoid H2-ready lock-in; specify low-temperature systems and heat-pump-ready emitters.

10) Decision points for non-traditional stock
- For PRC types (Cornish, Reema) with significant structural issues:
  - Apply gateway test: whole-life cost and liability vs. regeneration. Inputs: structural survey, costed remediation + energy works, decant costs, residual life, valuation impact, neighbourhood strategy.
  - If proceeding with retrofit: sequence structural remediation first, then EWI and services; insist on manufacturer/system warranties and independent clerk of works.

Immediate next steps (12-week plan)
- Finalise archetype library and risk categorisation for the 3,800 sub‑C homes.
- Commission RC-led assessments for first 1,000 homes, prioritising damp/mould and high bills.
- Launch two pathfinder packages: a) 150 solid-wall terraces EWI + ventilation; b) 150 No-Fines EWI; plus a PRC structural+EWI pilot (50 homes).
- Set procurement for PAS 2035-compliant designers/installers with non‑trad experience.
- Engage planners/heritage on priority streets and initiate DNO dialogue for 2027+ heat pump clusters.
- Approve programme KPIs: homes to C+, average heat demand reduction, IAQ scores, defects <2%, resident satisfaction >85%.

This pathway aligns capital delivery with PAS 2035 assurance, addresses the specific risks of solid-wall and non‑traditional homes, and builds a credible glidepath to EPC C by 2030 and net zero by 2050.

Here’s a pragmatic 2026–2030 delivery pathway to reach net zero (Scopes 1–2) for a mixed corporate estate, designed for a unitary authority with £8m/yr core capital and opportunistic PSDS bids. It sequences no‑regrets fabric and controls, prioritises high‑impact gas displacement, manages listed-building constraints, and de-risks grid, supply chain, and policy uncertainties.

1) Starting point and success conditions
- Estate: 180 buildings, 320,000 m2. EPC average D; ~30% E/F. High gas intensity (pools/leisure, depots with DHW/heating), heritage constraints on 4 civic/historic buildings.
- Emissions: ~18 ktCO2e/yr; ~65% from gas heat/DHW.
- Financial envelope: Core £8m/year capital (40m over 2026–2030) + competitive PSDS (assume two successful rounds totalling £12–20m if shovel‑ready).
- Energy prices and grid decarbonisation: electricity grid carbon intensity falling through 2030; gas prices volatile. Electrification plus demand reduction gives most CO2e reduction this period.
- Dependencies: Distribution network capacity, planning/listed building consent, supply chain capacity, PSDS timelines, procurement, internal project management resourcing, decant/operational windows.

2) Strategic principles
- Prioritise measures with: a) largest tCO2e impact per £ and per week of programme time, b) readiness for PSDS grant rules, c) future‑proofing (fabric first, low‑temp heat, smart controls).
- Segment buildings into archetypes: pools/leisure; 1960s–70s civic offices; Victorian libraries; depots; historic civic buildings.
- Adopt heat electrification as default end‑state for all but genuinely unsuitable heritage assets where interim solutions (hybrid, networked heat, or specialist conservation approaches) are needed.
- Pair heat pumps with load-reduction (fabric + controls + zoning) to reach 45–55°C flow temps where feasible.
- Scale enabling measures: metering, BMS upgrades, sub‑metering, water efficiency, refrigerant management, and grid readiness (LV/HV upgrades).
- Active energy management: central bureau with analytics to lock in 10–15% savings before capex hits site.
- Offsite renewables PPA to neutralise residual electricity emissions by 2030 if onsite PV/efficiency cannot fully offset; retain REC/REGOs and align with GHG Protocol quality criteria.

3) Programme phasing 2026–2030
Phase 0: 2025–Q2 2026 – Mobilise, baseline, and de-risk
- Data and design:
  - Establish accurate baselines: calibrate energy models for top 50 emitters; install/validate sub-metering and AMR across >80% of load by Q2 2026.
  - Heat decarbonisation plans (HDPs) for top 30 emitters (leisure, big offices, depots) to RIBA 2/3.
  - EPC/EED audits to lift EPC E/F to at least D by 2027 for MEES risk mitigation.
- Governance and procurement:
  - Create a Decarbonisation PMO with gateway control, standard specs, and NEC contracts; join a regional delivery framework to secure supply chain.
  - Secure DNO capacity studies and early budget quotations for 15–20 priority sites; place connection applications by Q3 2026.
- Quick wins (funded within 2026 £8m):
  - BMS optimisation and TRV/valve repairs; weather and occupancy compensation across 60 sites.
  - LED + controls to complete estate coverage where partial; target 10 GWh/yr electricity reduction by end‑2026.
  - DHW decarbonisation at offices/libraries/depots: point‑of‑use electric or ambient‑loop HP water heaters to allow gas boiler turndown in shoulder months.
  - Pool covers, VSDs on pumps/fans, AHU rebalancing in leisure.
- Funding readiness:
  - Prepare PSDS‑ready RIBA 3/4 designs for at least £20–30m of packages (ASHP/WSHP, fabric, PV, BMS) with carbon and kWh evidence.

Phase 1: Q3 2026–2027 – No‑regrets and high‑IRR packages
- Fabric first on E/F archetypes:
  - Roof/cavity/soffit insulation, secondary glazing where heritage constraints exist, air‑tightness works. Target 20–30% heat loss reduction in 1960s–70s offices and libraries.
- Controls and zoning:
  - BMS replacements/retrofits at top 25 energy sites; room booking integration for civic offices; CO2‑based ventilation control; weather compensation; setpoint rationalisation.
- Partial electrification:
  - Replace gas-fired DHW with HP/electric at all offices/libraries/depots by end‑2027.
  - Deploy packaged ASHPs for smaller sites (<200 kWth) where envelope allows 50–55°C flow.
- PV + storage wave 1:
  - Rooftop PV on structurally suitable offices, depots, leisure centres; prioritise behind‑the‑meter self‑consumption. Pilot 1–2 MWh Li‑ion batteries on leisure centres to manage peak demands and HP load shifting.
- Expected impact by end‑2027:
  - 20–25% CO2e reduction vs baseline (to ~13.5–14.5 kt), with gas share falling below 50%.

Phase 2: 2027–2028 – Major heat decarbonisation at leisure and large offices
- Leisure centres (pools) – biggest gas loads:
  - Convert 3–4 largest pools to heat pumps:
    - Option A: Air‑to‑water cascade ASHPs sized for 60–70% peak + electric top‑up; latent/condensing dehumidification with heat recovery; pool water HPs; reject heat capture from refrigeration/AC.
    - Option B: Water‑source HP using river/ground/abstraction where feasible; requires EA consent and capex lead time.
  - Fabric: pool hall air‑tightness, destratification fans, improved covers, AHU heat recovery upgrades.
  - Electrical enabling: new LV panels/transformers where needed; demand limiting and thermal stores to flatten peaks.
- Large 1960s–70s civic offices:
  - Rebalance emitters for low‑temp operation; fan‑coil or radiator upsizing where necessary; convert to multi‑split VRF with heat recovery or central ASHPs depending on life‑cycle and refrigerant policy.
  - Consider ambient‑temperature heat network across co‑located campus buildings (civic cluster + library) with central HP plant.
- PV + storage wave 2:
  - Continue roll‑out; target 5–7 MWp cumulative by end‑2028 if roofs/ground allow; integrate with HP load and EV depots.
- Expected impact by end‑2028:
  - 45–55% CO2e reduction vs baseline (to ~8–10 kt); gas share <30%.

Phase 3: 2028–2029 – Deep retrofit and heritage pathway
- Victorian libraries and historic civic buildings:
  - Fabric: internal insulation with vapour‑open systems, secondary glazing, draught‑proofing compatible with conservation.
  - Heat: low‑visual‑impact ASHPs (e.g., monobloc with remote condensers), or shared ambient loop serving multiple heritage buildings; consider hybrid (HP + retained boiler as frost/peak back‑up) only if absolutely necessary and with a gas phase‑out backstop by 2032.
  - Planning/listed building: early, iterative engagement with conservation officers; mock‑ups and reversible fixings.
- Depots and workshops:
  - Radiant gas heaters replaced with high‑bay electric IR or air‑to‑air HPs; destratification; fabric doors/fast‑acting shutters; EV fleet depot charging load management integrating with on‑site PV.
- Refrigerant management:
  - Policy to use lower‑GWP refrigerants (R290/R32 or HFOs) where safe; leak detection; F‑gas compliance and end‑of‑life recovery.
- Expected impact by end‑2029:
  - 65–75% CO2e reduction vs baseline (to ~4.5–6 kt). Remaining emissions primarily from hardest‑to‑treat heritage/pools peaks and residual gas backup, plus grid electricity.

Phase 4: 2029–2030 – Final push to net zero
- Mop‑up electrification:
  - Replace remaining gas plant; remove redundant gas services where possible to avoid standing charges.
  - Thermal storage and control refinements to achieve low‑temp heating everywhere feasible.
- Onsite renewables and offsite PPA:
  - Max out remaining PV capacity (subject to structural and planning limits); explore ground‑mount at depots/estate land if available.
  - Execute additionality‑strong PPA (new‑build wind/solar) sized to 100% of post‑efficiency electricity demand; include matching strategy (annual or, ideally, hourly by 2030 if procurement allows).
- Residuals and certification:
  - For any residual hard‑to‑eliminate combustion (e.g., heritage exemptions), use high‑quality, short‑lived carbon removals as a last resort with annual phase‑down plan and disclosure.
- Verification:
  - Third‑party M&V per IPMVP; publish annual progress; maintain asset‑level dashboards.

4) Capital plan and indicative split (core £40m + PSDS £12–20m)
- Enabling and controls: £6–8m (BMS, metering, valves, zoning, DNO upgrades where minor)
- Fabric retrofits: £10–14m (offices/libraries/depots; specialist heritage treatments)
- Heat pumps and DHW electrification: £22–28m (including plantrooms, emitters, thermal stores)
- PV + limited storage: £8–12m (6–10 MWp cumulative; 3–5 MWh storage targeted at leisure/depots)
- Professional fees, PMO, surveys, consents, contingency: £6–8m
Note: Pursue PSDS primarily for whole‑building HP + fabric + controls at leisure centres and large offices; match‑fund with core capital. Keep shovel‑ready pipeline to flex with award timing.

5) Expected carbon trajectory (order‑of‑magnitude)
- Start 2025: 18 ktCO2e/yr (65% gas)
- End‑2026: 15–16 kt (data/bureau, LED, DHW, BMS, some HPs)
- End‑2027: 13–14 kt (fabric upgrades, small/medium HPs, PV1)
- End‑2028: 8–10 kt (leisure/large office HP conversions, PV2)
- End‑2029: 4.5–6 kt (heritage/depots, optimisation)
- 2030 operational net zero: residual 2–4 kt offset by additional renewables PPA and minimal removals; plan to eliminate remaining combustion by 2032 where heritage constraints delay.

6) Dependencies and key risks
- Grid capacity and connection delays:
  - Risk: DNO capacity or long‑lead connections; HP electrification and PV export constraints.
  - Mitigation: Early applications (2026), deploy demand management, thermal storage, behind‑the‑meter PV/batteries, staggered commissioning, consider private wire for clusters.
- Supply chain and lead times:
  - Risk: HP plant, switchgear, transformers, specialist heritage materials.
  - Mitigation: Framework agreements, pre‑procurement market engagement, lotting strategy, advance orders, modular plantrooms.
- Planning and heritage consent:
  - Risk: Visual impact, fabric interventions refused, programme slippage.
  - Mitigation: Early conservation officer dialogue, heritage impact assessments, reversible designs, discrete plant location, acoustic studies.
- MEES and compliance:
  - Risk: EPC E/F buildings restricted for letting/occupation changes; funding eligibility linked to EPC uplift.
  - Mitigation: Prioritise E/F uplift by 2027 through fabric/lighting/controls; retest EPCs post‑works; maintain a MEES compliance register.
- PSDS funding uncertainty:
  - Risk: Bid rounds and criteria shifts; spend windows tight.
  - Mitigation: Maintain shovel‑ready RIBA 3/4 designs; phasing plans aligned to PSDS timelines; ability to re‑scope to core capital if bids fail.
- Performance gap:
  - Risk: HPs underperform due to high flow temps/controls; tenant override.
  - Mitigation: Commissioning codes, seasonal tuning, M&V, heat curve optimisation, operator training, service level KPIs tied to COP/SPF.
- Cost inflation and budget constraint:
  - Risk: Capex escalation, competing council priorities.
  - Mitigation: Portfolio cost control, value engineering, standardised kits of parts, bundling for scale discounts, whole‑life cost cases.
- Health and safety, pool downtime:
  - Risk: Programme clashes with service delivery.
  - Mitigation: Phased works, holiday shutdowns, temporary boilers/plant, stakeholder comms.
- Refrigerant/F‑gas policy changes:
  - Risk: Tighter rules on high‑GWP refrigerants.
  - Mitigation: Specify low‑GWP now; design for easy refrigerant replacement.

7) Governance, delivery model, and monitoring
- PMO with clear roles: client rep, cost control, carbon accountant, technical assurance, procurement lead, planning/heritage specialist.
- Gateway process: feasibility (RIBA 1–2) → business case → design assurance (RIBA 3–4) → delivery (RIBA 5) → seasonal commissioning (RIBA 6) → performance guarantee (Year 1).
- Performance contracting: Consider EPC/ESCO or energy‑as‑a‑service for leisure centres to guarantee kWh and COP, with pain/gain.
- Data and reporting:
  - Estate‑wide energy bureau with analytics; sub‑metering >80% coverage by 2027.
  - Publish annual carbon and energy intensity per m2 by archetype; align with SECR and TCFD.
  - Integrate with corporate risk register and audit.

8) Site archetype playbooks (summary)
- Leisure centres with pools: WSHP/ASHP cascades, DHW HPs, dehumidification with heat recovery, thermal storage, PV + batteries, pool covers, AHU upgrades. Electrify first 3–4 big sites for max CO2e impact.
- 1960s–70s civic offices: Fabric (roof/façade/air‑tightness), BMS, emitter upgrades, ASHPs or VRF with heat recovery; PV; DHW electrification.
- Victorian libraries: Internal insulation (vapour‑open), secondary glazing, small monobloc ASHPs, DHW HPs; careful controls to maintain conservation conditions.
- Depots: Fast doors, destratification, ASHP/air‑to‑air HPs, electric IR where spot heat needed; PV canopies for fleet charging; DHW point‑of‑use electric.
- Historic civic (incl. Grade II): Minimal‑impact fabric, secondary glazing, ambient loop/shared HPs, or hybrid with clear sunset; controls and monitoring prioritised; early heritage consent.

9) What to decide in 2026
- Approve portfolio heat electrification strategy and design standards (flow temps, refrigerant policy, metering, controls).
- Authorise DNO applications for 15–20 sites and allocate enabling capex.
- Fund PMO and technical assurance; place framework procurements.
- Green‑light Phase 1 no‑regrets works and PSDS bid pipeline to RIBA 3/4.
- Start PPA market testing and legal route for 2029–2030 supply.

If executed with strong governance and early enabling works, the council can reduce operational emissions by ~70% by end‑2029, with the remaining footprint covered by additional renewables PPA and minimal high‑quality removals to claim net zero for the corporate estate in 2030, while continuing to eliminate the final residual combustion soon after.

Here’s a practical, costed pathway to 2050 net-zero direct emissions that fits a typical trust’s funding reality, addresses risk (RAAC, PFI, CLASP), and aligns with DfE’s climate-adaptation 2030 milestone. The emphasis is on demand reduction first, smart sequencing, blended funding, and standardisation across sites.

1) Establish the trust-wide foundation (Year 1–2)
- Governance and targets:
  - Set trust-wide carbon budget to 2050 with 5-year carbon caps (e.g., −50% by 2035 vs 2023 baseline; −75% by 2040).
  - Create a Board-approved Net Zero & Resilience Policy and a Design Guide (heat pump-ready, fabric-first standards, LED spec, controls, PV, ventilation, embodied carbon, biodiversity).
  - Appoint a Head of Decarbonisation/Estates PMO; require every project to produce a whole-life carbon and cost case.

- Data, audits, prioritisation:
  - AMR/half-hourly meters on electricity and gas across all sites; sub-meter large secondaries.
  - Dynamic thermal models and heat-loss surveys for a representative sample of each archetype; EPC/SBEM refresh for all.
  - Trust-wide asset register: boiler age/efficiency, controls, distribution, roof condition/structural capacity, electrical headroom, glazing, U-values, ventilation, BMS presence/age, RAAC status.
  - Create a ranked pipeline using a marginal abatement cost curve (MACC) and risk scoring (H&S/RAAC > statutory > energy savings > education continuity).
  - Build a standard M&V plan (IPMVP Option C for large sites, B for packages).

- Quick wins and enablers (within existing SCA):
  - LED + controls across all schools (target <3-year payback, often 20–30% electrical cut).
  - BMS tune-ups/timeclock rationalisation; TRV repair; night set-back; deadband widening; CO2-controlled ventilation where compatible.
  - Hot water: fit point-of-use electric for low-demand basins to eliminate summer gas.
  - Draught-proofing; roof/loft top-ups where safe; pipework/valve insulation.
  - Low-cost resilience: shading films/blinds in overheating classrooms; leak detection; flood risk checks.

2) Tackle highest risk and highest energy first (Years 1–5)
- Safety and compliance:
  - RAAC assessment and mitigation first. Align decarbonisation with RAAC remediation to avoid abortive works; piggy-back fabric upgrades when ceilings/roofs are opened.

- CLASP-frame secondaries (1960s) – phased deep retrofit pilots:
  - Target 3–4 exemplar CLASP secondaries first (largest loads, worst EPCs).
  - Fabric-first package:
    - Roof replacement/overclad with warm-deck insulation (bring to ~0.15–0.18 W/m2K), make PV-ready with fixings and cableways.
    - External wall overcladding/insulation system suited to steel frames; address thermal bridges; upgrade glazing to low-e double/secondary where replacement impractical.
    - Air-tightness works; compartmentalisation to enable zoned heating.
  - Services:
    - Replace end-of-life boilers with high-temperature-ready heat emitters (oversize radiators/fan convectors) as part of a heat-pump transition plan.
    - Install variable speed drives, weather compensation, proper zoning, demand-controlled ventilation.
    - Pilot air-to-water heat pumps on blocks with lowest flow temp after fabric upgrades; retain hybrid/backup where necessary initially.
  - On-site generation and storage:
    - 200–500 kWp PV arrays per large secondary (subject to roof/structural capacity), export agreements, and future battery-readiness; fit 50–200 kWh batteries on two pilots to reduce peak import.
  - Funding mix:
    - Condition (roof, RAAC) via CIF/SCA, energy uplift via DfE GGF/Salix PSDS (if available), plus power purchase agreements (PPA) for PV where capex-limited.

- Victorian primaries – staged, low-intrusion upgrades:
  - Insulate roofs/lofts, secondary glazing on heritage windows, airtightness/sealing focused on doors and floor perimeters.
  - Convert DHW to point-of-use or dedicated small heat pumps (to decouple from space heating season).
  - Plan for low-temperature emitters in rooms with fabric upgrades first; small modular air-to-water or air-to-air heat pumps as pilots.

3) PFI-secondaries strategy (contracts to 2035)
- Engage PFI SPV now:
  - Create an Energy Variation Protocol: agree energy targets, pain/gain share, and lifecycle alignment.
  - Use change mechanism to add PV (via private wire), LED, BMS optimisation, and improved controls. Negotiate neutral or positive unitary charge impacts via shared savings.
  - Map end-of-term condition requirements so post-2035 heat pump conversion is “shovel-ready”: emitter upgrades, electrical capacity uplifts, roof PV prewiring can be scheduled as lifecycle replacements.
  - Explore third-party funded PV (PPA) that sits outside capex constraints but reduces bills/emissions immediately.

4) Develop a scalable retrofit standard and rollout (Years 3–10)
- Trust Retrofit Playbooks by archetype (Victorian, CLASP, modern, PFI):
  - Standard details for overclad, window upgrades, roof PV layouts, BMS templates, metering, preferred heat pump models/sizes, buffer/emitters, and commissioning checklists.
  - Procurement frameworks with performance guarantees (kWh/m2 targets), soft landings, and M&V.

- Sequencing principle:
  1) Fabric and controls to reduce heat demand 30–50%.
  2) Electrification-readiness: emitters, flow temperatures ≤50–55°C, electrical upgrades, 3-phase where needed.
  3) Generation and flexibility: PV first, then batteries where tariffs justify.
  4) Heat pump conversion at end-of-life of gas plant, avoiding stranded assets.

5) Funding and business case
- Core SCA (~£1.5m/yr):
  - Prioritise: roof replacements with insulation and PV-ready detailing; LED; BMS and controls; critical fabric; enabling works for future heat pumps (emitters, pipework zones).
  - Aim for 60–70% of SCA on measures with <7-year payback; ringfence ~30% for enabling and resilience.

- CIF and DfE GGF/Salix:
  - Use data-led bids from pilot outcomes; package projects to hit cost/carbon sweet spots (e.g., roof+overclad+PV).
  - Emphasise risk (RAAC, end-of-life boilers), energy/cost savings, and education continuity.

- Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) and green tariffs:
  - Use rooftop PV PPAs where capex is constrained; retain option to buy out at year 10–15.
  - Consider offsite sleeved PPA for residual electricity once electrified, to hedge price and ensure REGO-backed supply.

- Revenue savings recycling:
  - Establish an internal Reinvestment Fund from verified energy savings (e.g., 50% of year-1 savings ringfenced to future projects).

6) Emissions reduction trajectory (indicative)
- Baseline: 9 kt CO2e/yr; EPC average D; 180,000 m2 (~50 kgCO2e/m2).
- By 2028 (quick wins + partial fabric + PV on 10–12 largest roofs):
  - 20–30% electricity reduction via LED/controls.
  - 10–15% heat reduction via fabric/controls.
  - 2–3 MWp PV installed (2–2.5 GWh/yr).
  - Net reduction: ~20–25% (to ~6.8–7.2 kt).
- By 2030 (pilot deep retrofits + more PV + partial electrification):
  - 4–6 CLASP blocks deeply retrofitted; first tranche of heat pumps serving 15–20% of heat demand.
  - Total PV 4–6 MWp; batteries at 3–5 sites.
  - Aggregate reduction: ~35–45% (to ~5.0–5.8 kt).
  - Deliver climate-adaptation upgrades: overheating mitigation, drainage/SuDS, shade/trees, critical power resilience.
- By 2035 (PFI contract end; major pivot):
  - Convert 3 PFI secondaries to heat pumps as lifecycle events; extend deep retrofit to majority of large secondaries.
  - PV 8–10 MWp across trust; time-of-use/control optimisation.
  - Reduction: ~60–70% (to ~2.7–3.6 kt).
- By 2040–45:
  - Complete heat pump roll-out to remaining primaries/secondaries.
  - Replace remaining gas point sources; remove/abate catering gas if feasible; deploy further storage/flex.
  - Reduction: ~85–95% (to ≤1.3 kt), residuals offset or eliminated via final measures.
- 2050: Net zero direct emissions (Scope 1), with decarbonised grid and residual eliminations.

7) Climate adaptation plan (to meet 2030 milestone)
- Overheating:
  - CIBSE TM52/TM59 assessments for refurbished blocks; shading, night purging, plus reflective roofs and planting.
- Flood and drainage:
  - Site-specific flood risk plans, backflow valves, sump pumps, raised plant, SuDS (rain gardens, permeable).
- Water efficiency:
  - AMR on water; low-flow fixtures; leak detection; rainwater harvesting where viable.
- Resilience and continuity:
  - Critical rooms with improved ventilation/filtration; small backup power for ICT/comms; heatwave action plans.

8) Technical standards and KPIs
- Target energy intensity post-retrofit:
  - Primaries: 80–100 kWh/m2/yr total delivered energy.
  - Secondaries: 110–140 kWh/m2/yr.
- Heat pump-ready:
  - After fabric works, design for 45–50°C flow at −2 to −3°C external design temp.
- PV target:
  - Fill suitable roof area to 30–50% of annual kWh consumption per site initially; expand after electrification.
- Procurement:
  - Performance-based contracts with guaranteed kWh savings and seasonal COP/SPF targets.
- M&V:
  - Quarterly dashboards; variance analysis; publish annual Trust Sustainability Report.

9) Risk management
- RAAC: do not install heavy PV or overclad on suspect panels until remediated/engineer-signed.
- Grid capacity: early engagement with DNO; cluster applications for connections; consider on-site peak lopping via batteries.
- Asbestos/heritage: programme surveys early, coordinate with fabric works.
- Educational disruption: plan summer/half-term interventions; modular plantrooms; phased block-by-block works.

10) Next 12 months action list
- Approve policy, appoint PMO lead, set carbon budgets.
- Complete metering rollout and audits for top 10 energy sites.
- Deliver trust-wide LED and BMS optimisation package.
- Submit two CIF bids: (1) roof/RAAC remediation with insulation and PV-ready; (2) boiler EoL replacement with low-temp emitters and HP-enabling works.
- Prepare two GGF/Salix bids for CLASP deep retrofit pilots with partial HP and PV.
- Launch three PV PPA projects on the best roofs.
- Publish adaptation plan for 2030 with site-specific risk registers.

This pathway prioritises safety and resilience, locks in immediate low-cost savings, and times major electrification to funding windows (PFI end and lifecycle stages), keeping within SCA constraints while leveraging external funds and PPAs to reach net zero by 2050.

Below is a pragmatic, security-aware decarbonisation pathway for the North West HMPPS cluster that hits the 50% reduction by 2032 and sets up a credible glidepath to net zero by 2050. It prioritises highest-return heat and hot-water interventions, grid decarbonisation leverage, and delivery within typical MoJ/HMPPS funding/assurance routes (ETP + PSDS).

Starting point and constraints
- Baseline: 24 ktCO2e/yr; ~75% from gas (space heating + very high DHW for showers, laundry, kitchens). 24/7 operation.
- Estate: 8 prisons, mixed age/condition: 2 Victorian Cat B locals (complex fabric/services), 4 1960–80s Cat C (often poor insulation, large plant rooms), 2 modern resettlement (post-2010; better fabric, BMS-ready).
- Security: Limited tolerance for extensive external ground works; strong preference for internal-plantroom, roof-mounted, or modular solutions; phased works to maintain resilience.
- Funding: ~£12m/yr cluster average; blend of core capex and PSDS (Salix) for non-domestic public sector decarb, especially heat pumps/heat networks/controls/fabric.

Overall strategy
1) Reduce heat and hot-water loads first where fast and non-disruptive.
2) Electrify heat with high-availability heat pumps sized and staged for DHW priority, exploiting high-efficiency preheat + top-up architectures.
3) Decarbonise electricity via on-site PV plus grid greening; shift loads to off-peak/low-carbon periods where operationally acceptable.
4) Retain gas as resilient back-up initially, then progressively decommission or convert to bio/biogas if credible supply chain emerges.
5) Target high-impact anchor sites early (modern prisons and the best plant rooms at the 1960–80s sites); schedule complex Victorian conversions later, pairing with envelope and zonal heat network upgrades.

Emissions reduction trajectory (illustrative)
- 2026: -10 to -15% vs baseline (quick wins, controls, DHW optimisation, PV wave 1)
- 2028: -25 to -30% (site-scale heat pump preheat systems for DHW; partial space heat electrification at 2–3 sites)
- 2030: -40 to -45% (cluster heat networks at two prisons, further space heat pumps, laundry heat recovery)
- 2032: ≥ -50% (full DHW electrification at all sites; majority of space heating at modern + 2–3 of the 1960–80s sites electrified; PV/battery scaled)
- 2050: Net zero (complete phaseout of fossil boilers or conversion to verified zero-carbon fuels; residuals offset per MoJ policy)

Priority measures and packages
A) No-regrets efficiency and controls (Years 1–3; low capex, low disruption)
- BMS upgrades and zoning: Standardise control strategies across the cluster. Night set-backs in non-critical zones; weather compensation; occupancy-based schedules for admin/education blocks.
- Hot water temperature and flow optimisation: Maintain Legionella compliance while avoiding excessive setpoints; fit thermostatic mixing valves with accurate control.
- Variable speed drives (VSDs) for pumps/fans; balance distribution systems.
- Tighten metering: Sub-meter DHW, kitchens, laundries; install heat meters on primary circuits to baseline and verify PSDS projects.

B) DHW decarbonisation first (Years 1–5; biggest gas driver, 24/7 loads)
- Heat pump-led DHW systems:
  - Central plantroom air-to-water or water-to-water heat pumps providing 55–65°C bulk preheat to large buffer vessels; top-up to 70°C using high-temperature heat pumps or periodic electric pasteurisation cycles. Maintain weekly thermal disinfection or equivalent per HSG274.
  - For Victorian and 1960–80s sites with cramped plantrooms, use modular skid-mounted units to minimise on-site works; for modern sites, integrate into existing plant with minimal adaptation.
- Waste heat recovery:
  - Laundry: Install high-temp drain water heat recovery (DWHR) and tumble dryer exhaust heat recovery to preheat incoming cold make-up or feed the DHW preheat loop.
  - Kitchens: Plate heat exchangers on dishwashers/waste-heat streams where feasible; capture refrigeration condenser heat where plantrooms allow.
- Target: Convert all eight sites’ DHW to heat pump preheat by 2029, fully displacing gas for DHW by 2031.

C) Space heating electrification in stages (Years 2–10 initial; then expand)
- Modern resettlement prisons (post-2010): Early adopters for full air-to-water or water-to-water heat pumps, often compatible with lower flow temps (45–55°C). Consider hybrid arrangement with existing boilers as peak/backup for smooth transition.
- 1960–80s Cat C: Phase 1: Low-temp conversion of select blocks with emitter checks (radiator upsizing where needed), plus secondary return temperature reduction to lift heat pump COP. Phase 2: Extend to remaining blocks as fabric/envelope are modestly improved.
- Victorian Cat B locals: Space heating electrification later, combined with:
  - Internal wall insulation in targeted zones (cells may be challenging; focus on admin, education, healthcare, workshops first).
  - Heat network “spine” splitting into temperature tiers; deploy high-temp heat pumps where low-temp is infeasible.
- Outside air source vs water source:
  - Prefer air-to-water with acoustic enclosures on roofs/yards to avoid deep ground works.
  - Where site has cooling towers/chilled water or nearby water bodies/large surface drains, evaluate water-source HP for better COP and smaller footprint.
- Target: By 2032, fully electrify space heating at both modern sites and 2–3 of the 1960–80s sites; retain hybrid/backup on others. Complete cluster-wide space heat electrification by 2040–2045.

D) Site heat networks and plant consolidation (Years 3–10)
- Create or reinforce low- to medium-temperature site heat networks to serve multiple blocks from central high-efficiency heat pump energy centres, simplifying maintenance in secure plant areas and reducing the number of flues/rooftop units.
- At large sites, design for future connection of additional buildings and for seasonal storage later (see H).

E) On-site renewables and flexibility (Years 1–8)
- Solar PV:
  - Roof-mounted first across modern and 1960–80s buildings; then carport PV in staff car parks (security-friendly).
  - Avoid ground-mount in secure perimeters unless operationally acceptable.
  - Cluster target: 8–12 MWp cumulative by 2032, phased with roof replacements and PSDS windows. Expect 7–9 GWh/yr yield, directly offsetting HP and DHW loads.
- Battery energy storage systems (BESS):
  - 0.5–2 MWh per large site to time-shift PV for DHW evening peaks and shave import peaks to control DUoS/Capacity charges; place in secure plant compounds.
- Demand flexibility:
  - Preheat DHW buffers and thermal stores during low-carbon/low-tariff periods; integrate with DSR services where policy permits.

F) Fabric and distribution upgrades where they unlock heat pump performance (Years 2–12)
- Focused, quick-return works: loft/cavity insulation where present; door/window sealing; TRVs and hydraulic balancing to allow lower flow temps.
- Targeted emitter upgrades in blocks slated for heat pumps to hit 45–55°C flow temps.
- Victorian blocks: selective internal insulation in non-cell areas during planned refurb windows.

G) Residual gas and transition fuels (Years 5–15)
- Maintain smaller, high-efficiency condensing boilers as N+1 resilience in early phases. Reduce seasonal hours of use as HP share grows.
- Evaluate biomethane/green gas certificates as an interim accounting measure only if aligned with MoJ policy and additionality standards; avoid hardware lock-in.

H) Long-term enablers toward net zero (2030–2050)
- Large thermal stores (50–200 m3) at biggest sites to load shift HP operation and enable very high renewable penetration.
- Aquifer/ground thermal storage or borehole arrays only where security and ground conditions allow; otherwise stick to modular air-source and water-source HPs.
- Explore electrification of kitchen process heat with high-efficiency electric combi ovens and induction; specify HP-fed plate washers.
- Fleet and site logistics electrification synergies (shared transformers, smart charging) to strengthen business case for substation upgrades.

Programme, phasing, and funding alignment
- 2026–2028 (Wave 1–2 PSDS + ETP):
  - Cluster-wide BMS/controls/meters and VSDs.
  - DHW preheat HPs at 3–4 sites (prioritise modern + most energy-intensive 1960–80s).
  - PV wave 1: 3–4 MWp across best roofs; small BESS pilots.
  - Laundry and kitchen heat recovery at two largest laundries/kitchens.
- 2028–2030:
  - Extend DHW HPs to remaining sites; implement electric pasteurisation strategy.
  - Full space heat HP at both modern prisons; hybrid conversion at 1–2 Cat C.
  - PV wave 2 to 7–8 MWp total; BESS at 3 sites; first site heat network upgrade.
- 2030–2032:
  - Additional space heat HP conversions (total 3–5 sites largely electrified).
  - Thermal stores at 2–3 sites for flexibility.
  - PV to 8–12 MWp; cluster-wide DHW off gas.
  - Achieve ≥50% emissions reduction vs baseline.
- 2032–2040:
  - Complete space heat electrification at remaining Cat C; begin Victorian main blocks with targeted fabric upgrades and medium-temp networks.
- 2040–2050:
  - Final phase-out of fossil back-up; residual emissions neutralised per MoJ net-zero approach.

Indicative impact and costs (high-level order of magnitude)
- Quick wins and controls: £3–5m cluster-wide; 5–8% savings.
- DHW HP conversions + heat recovery: £18–25m across 8 sites; 20–25% cluster reduction.
- Space heat HPs (first 4–5 sites, partial to full): £25–40m; 15–20% reduction.
- PV 8–12 MWp + BESS: £10–18m; 5–10% reduction (direct + enabling).
- Fabric/enablers/thermal stores/heat networks: £15–25m over a decade; 5–10% reduction enablement.
Total over 8–10 years: £70–110m, phased at ~£8–14m/yr average, aligned with £12m/yr allocation plus PSDS match-funding. Apply PSDS primarily to HPs, heat networks, metering/BMS, and PV; use ETP for fabric, resilience, and enabling works.

Risk management and security considerations
- Prefer internal plantroom and rooftop installs; modular skids to minimise time in secure yards.
- Plan works block-by-block to maintain heating and DHW redundancy; schedule pasteurisation cycles and changeovers outside peak shower times.
- Acoustic design for ASHPs; anti-climb and ballistic-rated enclosures where required.
- Early DNO engagement for capacity upgrades; sequence PV/BESS and HP rollouts to manage demand.
- Legionella and water hygiene sign-off embedded in design and O&M.

Governance, data, and assurance
- Establish a cluster energy masterplan with site-by-site heat load profiles, DHW draw profiles, and electrification readiness scores.
- Metering and M&V plan to verify PSDS outcomes and feed continuous optimisation.
- Standardised technical specs for HPs, buffers, controls, and PV/BESS across the cluster to speed procurement and maintenance.
- Develop a spares and training program for estates teams; remote monitoring contracts with clear KPIs.

What to do next (first 6–9 months)
- Complete cluster-wide heat and DHW audits; confirm DHW temperature regimes and pasteurisation approach.
- DNO capacity assessments and PV/BESS siting studies.
- PSDS-ready business cases for: DHW HPs at 3–4 priority sites; laundry/kitchen heat recovery; PV wave 1; BMS/meters.
- RIBA 2–3 designs for two heat pump energy centres (one modern, one 1960–80s) as exemplars.
- Procurement framework selection and enabling works plans (plantroom surveys, asbestos checks, structural checks for roof PV/plant).

This pathway focuses on fast, secure, high-impact DHW decarbonisation; scalable site heat pump energy centres; and PV/flex to control costs and grid impact—delivering the ≥50% cut by 2032 and a clear, fundable route to net zero by 2050.

Proposed decarbonisation pathway for HMCTS South East court estate (45 buildings, 150,000 m2; 7 ktCO2e/yr; EPC avg D)

Objectives
- Meet Greening Government Commitments: c.78% emissions reduction by 2035 (vs 2017/18 baseline) and net zero by 2050.
- Work within MoJ maintenance (~£3m/yr South East) and leverage PSDS/Salix, Heat Network Zones, and other funds.
- Balance heritage constraints (8 listed courts) with performance upgrades; tackle magistrates’ courts with poor fabric/overheating; standardise solutions for modern combined centres.

Overall strategy
- Fabric first where feasible, then heat decarbonisation, controls, and on-site renewables; apply demand reduction to lower heat pump sizes and cost.
- Segment estate into three archetypes with tailored playbooks: A) Listed Victorian/Edwardian crown courts; B) 1960s–80s magistrates’ courts; C) Modern combined court centres.
- Prioritise highest-emitting and easiest-to-abate sites first to maximise early carbon and cost savings; create a rolling programme aligned to PSDS windows.
- Centralised program management with standard specifications, metering/measurement and verification (M&V), and regional delivery partners.

Programme phasing and targets
- 2026–2028 (Phase 1: no-regrets, data, quick wins): 20–25% CO2e reduction vs current.
- 2028–2031 (Phase 2: heat decarbonisation at priority sites, deeper fabric): reach ~50–60% reduction.
- 2031–2035 (Phase 3: complete main heat transitions, residual PV and controls): reach ≥78% reduction.
- 2035–2050 (Phase 4: residuals, grid decarbonisation, offsets only for hard-to-abate heritage constraints near 2050).

Cross-estate enablers (start immediately)
- Data and metering: Install advanced sub-metering (heat/electricity/gas by zone/plant), BMS analytics, and half-hourly data feeds; build digital twins for top 15 emitters.
- Condition and decarb audits: ASHRAE Level 2 audits for all; heat decarbonisation feasibility (hydraulic design, emitter checks, space for plant).
- Controls/BMS: Standardise BMS, zone schedules, night set-backs, TRVs, CO2-based ventilation control. Target 8–12% savings estate-wide quickly.
- Refrigerants: Specify low-GWP refrigerants (R32/R290/CO2) in all replacements; maintenance to avoid leakage.
- Procurement framework: Pre-approve suppliers for heat pumps, fabric, PV, BMS; publish standard employer’s requirements to reduce design time.
- Planning/listed building engagement: Early liaison with conservation officers; prepare heritage impact assessments and reversible upgrade methodologies.

Archetype playbooks

A) Listed Victorian/Edwardian (8 Grade II/II*)
Challenges: heritage façades, single glazing, high ceilings, limited roof PV, aesthetic constraints. Often steam/radiators sized for high flow temps.

Measures (phased):
- Fabric/air-tightness (reversible/low-visual-impact):
  - Secondary glazing (magnetically attached or slimline heritage units) targeting whole-window U ≤1.8 W/m2K; shutters/blinds for solar control.
  - Loft/roof void top-up insulation; insulate attic floors where accessible; draught-proofing; fireplace dampers; underfloor insulation in accessible voids.
  - Internal wall insulation only where moisture-safe and non-significant spaces (lime plaster-compatible systems; hygrothermal modelling).
- Heating decarbonisation:
  - Transition to low-temp systems in stages: clean/flush and balance, oversize emitters in select rooms, add fan-coils where acceptable, enable 50–55°C flow temperatures initially.
  - Deploy high-temp heat pumps (80°C capable) only where emitters cannot be changed; consider cascade systems; retain limited gas backup short-term if needed.
  - Thermal stores and buffer tanks to manage peak demand; weather compensation and zone control critical.
- Ventilation and overheating:
  - Mixed-mode strategies, roof void extract, discreet window actuators with controls; internal shading; consider reversible ceiling fans; avoid visible external plant where possible.
- Renewables:
  - PV where non-visible roof slopes/ancillary buildings allow; consider PV slates only if viable; solar thermal for DHW where space permits.
- Expected savings: 35–55% site-level by 2035, higher if glazing/insulation accepted. Some residual emissions likely until grid fully decarbonises.

B) 1960s–80s magistrates’ courts (22)
Challenges: poor fabric, overheating, often all-air systems or electric resistance in parts, flat roofs, services at end-of-life.

Measures:
- Fabric:
  - Roof insulation (inverted roof systems), cavity/ETO cladding where architecturally acceptable; window replacement to modern double/triple low-e; airtightness works.
  - Solar control films/external brise-soleil to tackle overheating.
- HVAC:
  - Replace gas boilers with air-to-water heat pumps; if all-air, convert AHUs to low-temp coils with heat pumps; add heat recovery to ventilation.
  - Consider VRF/VRV to zonal spaces where water systems are impractical, but prioritise hydronic for longevity.
  - Hot water: point-of-use heat pump water heaters or central ASHP with storage; eliminate oversized circulation losses.
- Controls/LED:
  - LED and smart lighting controls throughout; BMS upgrades; CO2/DCV retrofits.
- Renewables:
  - Maximise PV on flat roofs; battery storage where export limits constrain; EV charging readiness.
- Embodied/roofing:
  - Align re-roofing cycles with PV and insulation to stack funding.
- Expected savings: 60–75% per site by 2035; many can reach near-zero operational emissions with PV + heat pumps as grid decarbonises.

C) Modern combined court centres (15)
Challenges: larger, more modern, better plant space; good PV potential.

Measures:
- Heat: Replace boilers with large modular air-to-water heat pumps (or water-source if viable); optimise existing LTHW systems to 45–55°C with emitter upgrades.
- Ventilation: High-efficiency heat recovery, demand control; upgrade AHUs/fans.
- Smart controls and sub-metering by zone; optimise setpoints.
- PV: Large arrays; consider PPAs or public sector leasing models.
- Expected savings: 55–70% quickly; strong PSDS candidates due to scale.

Sequenced delivery plan

Phase 1: 2026–2028 (quick wins and readiness)
- Portfolio actions:
  - LED and controls across estate; BMS optimisation; heat curve optimisation on boilers; water heating rationalisation; refrigerant leak checks.
  - Sub-metering rollout; M&V platform; staff/occupant engagement and operational policies (heating/cooling setpoints, on/off times).
- Site projects (PSDS-ready packages):
  - 8–10 highest-consuming magistrates/combined centres: roof insulation, PV, initial heat pump pilots (2–3 sites), AHU heat recovery retrofits.
- Capex: ~£12–18m over 3 years (blend MoJ £3m/yr + PSDS 50–70% grants).
- Impact: 1.5–2.0 ktCO2e/yr reduction.

Phase 2: 2028–2031 (scale heat decarb)
- Convert 12–15 additional sites to heat pumps, focusing on magistrates’ courts and combined centres with strong PV opportunities.
- Deep fabric packages on 8–10 magistrates’ courts (windows + façade + roof).
- Begin listed building heat pump deployments with reversible emitter upgrades; secondary glazing roll-out.
- Evaluate connections to any emerging heat networks in urban centres (if low-carbon supply assured).
- Capex: ~£35–45m (PSDS and SALIX loans; bundle across tranches).
- Impact: cumulative 3.5–4.2 ktCO2e/yr reduction vs baseline.

Phase 3: 2031–2035 (complete majority transitions)
- Remaining viable heat pump conversions; residual gas only where heritage/technical constraints persist.
- PV saturation on all practical roofs; limited battery storage.
- Advanced analytics for ongoing optimisation (5–10% additional savings).
- Capex: ~£25–35m.
- Outcome: Achieve ≥78% reduction by 2035 across portfolio, with a small number of listed sites at partial decarb pending further measures.

Phase 4: 2035–2050 (residuals and net zero)
- Tackle hard-to-abate heritage constraints with next-gen high-temp heat pumps, ambient loop networks, and innovative glazing/insulation that meet conservation guidance.
- Address remaining process loads, fleet EV transition for site vehicles, and procure 100% renewable electricity (additionality where possible).
- Residual emissions plan: high-quality, UK-based nature or engineered removals near 2050 for any unavoidable residuals.

Funding and business case
- Leverage PSDS for heat decarb and fabric (priority to worst EPCs and E-rated listed buildings).
- SALIX interest-free loans for invest-to-save measures with paybacks ≤10–12 years (LED, controls, PV).
- Bundle projects to cross-subsidise heritage sites with higher abatement costs using surplus savings from magistrates’/combined centres.
- Consider power purchase agreements (PPA) for larger PV where capex is constrained.
- Target whole-life cost optimisation: reduced maintenance from plant replacement cycles; factor avoided carbon costs and resilience benefits.

Risk and mitigation
- Planning/listed consent delays: engage early; use precedent case studies and reversible details.
- Grid capacity: apply for DNO capacity assessments early; stage electrification; add smart load management and limited storage.
- Heat pump performance: thorough hydraulic design, emitter checks, and commissioning; seasonal COP monitoring via M&V.
- Overheating/comfort: pair insulation with shading/ventilation; publish temperature policies; avoid winter over-heating from high setpoints.

Governance and delivery
- Establish a Decarbonisation PMO for the South East with a clear RACI, gateway approvals, and benefits tracking.
- Define standard KPIs: kWh/m2, kgCO2e/m2, comfort compliance, EPC uplift, £/tCO2e abated.
- Use a regional delivery partner framework with call-off for audits, design, and EPC/M&V.
- Report quarterly against Greening Government Commitments, aligned to MoJ sustainability reporting.

Indicative outcomes by 2035
- Electricity share of energy >80%; gas usage reduced by 85–95% across non-heritage sites.
- Portfolio emissions reduced from 7 ktCO2e/yr to ≤1.5 ktCO2e/yr (≥78% cut), with residuals primarily at 2–3 listed sites pending technical/planning solutions.
- EPC uplift: average from D to C/B for modern and magistrates’ courts; heritage improved to D/C where permissible via secondary glazing and controls.

Next steps (first 6–9 months)
- Commission portfolio-wide audits and metering plan; select 6 pilot sites (2 per archetype).
- Prepare PSDS-ready investment-grade proposals with shovel-ready designs for next funding window.
- Begin estate-wide controls optimisation and LED upgrades immediately.
- Start heritage engagement and consent strategy for the 8 listed courts with outline designs and risk logs.

Below is a practical, financeable pathway to reach net zero Scope 1+2 by 2035 for a UK cold‑chain 3PL with 12 sites (280,000 m2) dominated by refrigeration. It sequences interventions to cut demand and emissions early, replaces high‑GWP refrigerants, adds renewable supply and storage, and manages grid and policy risk. It assumes capex £8–10m/yr to 2035, with flexibility for opportunistic spend (e.g., when plant fails or incentives arise).

1) Baseline and key constraints
- Load: ~95 GWh/yr electricity; refrigeration ≈ 75% (≈71 GWh), other ≈ 24 GWh. Scope 1 likely small (backup gensets, gas boilers for offices/defrost in some chilled areas), but include fugitive refrigerants (very material for HFC sites).
- Emissions: ~28 ktCO2e/yr Scope 1+2. UK grid decarbonisation will help, but not fast enough to meet 2035 target without on‑site action.
- Refrigeration fleet: Legacy ammonia (NH3) plants from 1990s (likely screw compressors, two‑stage, economisers) and HFC‑404A systems awaiting F‑gas phase‑down compliance. 404A has very high GWP and is a regulatory and cost risk.
- Capex: £8–10m per year (≈ £80–100m to 2035).
- Customer pressure: SBTi‑aligned; expects near‑term absolute reductions and low reliance on unbundled EACs.

2) Strategy pillars and sequencing (high level)
- Pillar A: Demand reduction and system optimisation now (2026–2028), to shrink the problem and prepare sites for electrification and heat recovery.
- Pillar B: Refrigeration transition to natural refrigerants (NH3/CO2) with ultra‑low leak rates and high efficiency; phase out 404A by 2030 at the latest (frontload high‑GWP removals).
- Pillar C: Electrification and heat integration (defrost, space heat, DHW) using heat recovery and heat pumps to displace any gas/diesel.
- Pillar D: On‑site/off‑site renewables plus flexibility (BESS, demand response) to cut residual grid emissions cost‑effectively.
- Pillar E: High‑quality residuals: RE100‑grade procurement (UK‑located PPAs), minimal reliance on unbundled REGOs, and only limited, high‑quality offsets for hard‑to‑abate leakage to reach net zero by 2035.
- Pillar F: Data, controls, and governance to verify SBTi alignment; refrigerant leak management and MRV.

3) Detailed pathway and phasing
Years 1–2 (2026–2027): No‑regrets efficiency, risk removal, and portfolio planning
- Portfolio audit and design standards
  - Create a fleetwide refrigeration replacement roadmap and standard specs: NH3/CO2 cascade for deep‑frozen; transcritical CO2 with parallel compression + ejectors for chilled; or low‑charge packaged NH3 for medium temp; heat recovery integrated.
  - Rank sites by age, performance (kWh/m3), leakage, failure risk, grid capacity, solar/BESS potential, and planning constraints.
  - Establish design KPI targets: SEC for frozen ≤ 30–40 kWh/m3/yr; chilled ≤ 15–20 kWh/m3/yr; system COP/SEPR targets; leak rate ≤ 5%/yr (HFC) transitioning to <1%/yr (natural refrigerants).
- Immediate operational optimisations (1–2 year paybacks)
  - Setpoints and control tuning: tighten door interlocks, defrost scheduling, floating head/ suction optimisation, VSDs on evaporator/condenser fans and pumps, night blinds/strip curtains, dock seal improvements, occupancy/scheduling discipline.
  - Infiltration and envelope: rapid‑roll doors, air curtains for docks, repair gaskets, upgrade insulation on high‑loss sections, de‑ice protocols.
  - Submetering and analytics: install granular metering (compressors, fans, pumps, docks, HVAC, lighting), BMS/SCADA upgrades with alarms and automated reporting.
  - Lighting: complete LED + controls (likely mostly done but verify).
  - Expected savings: 10–15% on refrigeration electricity (≈7–10 GWh/yr) and 2–3 GWh on balance of plant; emissions cut 2–3 ktCO2e/yr.
- Refrigerant risk triage
  - Identify all R404A systems; start phased conversion prioritising highest leak/energy sites. For interim, drop‑in lower‑GWP blends (e.g., R448A/R449A) only where immediate replacement is impossible in <24 months; plan for full natural refrigerant conversion.
  - Implement enhanced leak detection (fixed sensors, weekly checks), certified maintenance, and refrigerant mass balance reporting to cut fugitive emissions quickly.
- Procurement foundation
  - Launch PPA process for 10–20 GWh/yr UK renewable electricity (wind/solar) commencing 2028–2029; structure as sleeved/virtual PPA with additionality and RE100 compliance. Keep REGOs as bridge only.
- Grid/flexibility groundwork
  - Apply for grid capacity reviews and connections upgrades where large plant replacements and EV charging (if relevant) will land.
  - Pre‑feasibility for BESS (1–2 MWh per large site) to enable TRIAD/DUoS/BSUoS and Dynamic services revenue, and to shape solar.

Years 3–6 (2028–2031): Major plant replacements, natural refrigerants, heat recovery, first wave of renewables and storage
- Replace/retrofit 404A and weakest ammonia plants (approx. 5–7 sites in first wave)
  - Frozen: NH3/CO2 cascade or low‑charge NH3 central plant with adiabatic condensers; brine/CO2 secondary loops as needed; VSD compressors; EC fans; floating pressures.
  - Chilled: Transcritical CO2 with parallel compression, gas cooler adiabatic assist; ejectors where viable; integrate medium/low temp as needed.
  - Heat recovery: Plate exchangers and desuperheaters to capture 30–50°C for DHW/space; add high‑temp CO2/NH3 heat pumps where load requires 55–70°C for defrost/office heat; remove gas-fired heaters/boilers where feasible.
  - Specify low charge, segregated plantrooms, leak detection, and safety systems; design for maintenance access to maintain efficiency.
  - Target 20–30% energy reduction vs baseline at retrofit sites; eliminate very high GWP fugitive risk.
- Site‑level electrification
  - Remove any remaining LPG/diesel space/water heating; convert to electric heat pumps using recovered heat where possible.
  - Evaluate battery forklifts/chargers scheduling to exploit off‑peak/onsite PV.
- On‑site solar and BESS rollout
  - Rooftop PV: 30–50 W/m2 practical potential; with 280,000 m2, theoretical gross ~8–14 MWp; consider structural checks, roof age, and cold‑store shading. Realistically deploy 6–10 MWp over multiple sites across 2028–2031.
  - BESS: 0.5–2 MWh per large site to shave peaks, time‑shift PV, and support demand response; co‑optimise with refrigeration load control.
- Off‑site renewable PPAs
  - Execute first 10–20 GWh/yr PPA; plan to scale to 60–80 GWh/yr by 2031 to cover majority of residual grid use after efficiency.
- Controls and analytics
  - Fleetwide advanced controls platform with central monitoring, AI‑assisted fault detection, and optimisation; continuous commissioning.
- Expected cumulative impact by 2031
  - Electricity use down 25–35% (to ~60–70 GWh/yr).
  - HFC phase‑down largely complete (>80% of 404A removed).
  - Scope 2 emissions down >60% via efficiency + PPAs + onsite PV; scope 1 fugitive emissions down sharply.

Years 7–9 (2032–2034): Complete HFC exit, optimise portfolio, deepen renewables, flexibility, and residual heat electrification
- Second wave of plant replacements (remaining 5–7 sites)
  - Complete transition to natural refrigerants across all sites; standardise spare parts, training, and remote diagnostics.
  - Upgrade any early‑wave retrofits with new control features (e.g., advanced ejectors, improved adiabatic systems) as tech matures.
- Expand PV/BESS
  - Grow onsite PV to practical maximum (target cumulative 10–15 MWp); scale BESS where economics prove (stacked revenues).
- Deepen PPAs
  - Layer additional UK PPAs to reach 100% annual consumption matched with additional renewable generation; pursue hourly/quarterly matching pilots where available to improve quality claims.
- Full electrification
  - Ensure no fossil backup for heat; replace legacy diesel gensets for backup with battery + renewable‑ready gensets or HVO as interim (accounting policy needed).
- Refrigerant leakage and MRV excellence
  - Achieve <1%/yr leak rate fleetwide; implement reclamation/recycling and end‑of‑life recovery contracts to avoid venting.
- Expected position end‑2034
  - Energy use ~55–65 GWh/yr; >90% electricity matched by additional renewables; natural refrigerants everywhere; minimal residual Scope 1.

2035: Net zero Scope 1+2
- Procure last increment of high‑quality renewable supply (hourly matched where feasible) to cover residuals.
- Address small residual emissions (e.g., standby genset tests, refrigerant lifecycle) with high‑quality, verifiable removals (durable carbon removal or UK nature‑based with strong MRV as allowed by customer/SBTi).
- Verification: third‑party assurance of GHG inventory, RE claims (RE100‑compliant), and refrigerant accounting.

4) Capex and economics (indicative)
- Refrigeration plant replacements: £3–6m per large site depending on scope; phase across 8–10 years aligned to capex envelope. Focus on highest energy/HFC first to maximise tCO2e reduced per £.
- PV: ~£600–900/kWp rooftop. A 10 MWp fleet implies £6–9m spread over multiple years.
- BESS: ~£300–450/kWh installed for 1–2 MWh/site scale by early 2030s; prioritise sites with grid constraints and best flexibility revenues.
- Controls, metering, doors/air seals/insulation upgrades: ~£2–4m across fleet in first two years.
- Expect blended paybacks 4–8 years on efficiency and controls; refrigeration replacements justified on compliance, risk, and energy savings (20–40% site savings), often 6–10 year payback but critical for HFC phase‑down and resilience. PPAs provide cost certainty and can be cost‑neutral or better vs rising grid costs.

5) Dependencies and enabling actions
- Grid capacity and planning
  - Early DNO engagement for sites receiving larger compressors, heat pumps, EV chargers, and BESS. Secure export/import capacity for PV/BESS; consider private wires if co‑located generation options arise.
- Planning and permitting
  - Rooftop PV, adiabatic condensers, external plant enclosures: ensure noise, visual, water use (adiabatic) and Legionella controls; comply with COMAH if applicable for ammonia, and Pressure Systems Safety Regulations.
- Water availability
  - For adiabatic/gas cooler assist, account for water permits, legionella risk management, and water treatment; include dry-mode performance for drought periods.
- Refrigerant and safety
  - Ammonia handling competence, leak detection, ventilation, emergency plans; training and contractor frameworks; DSEAR compliance. For CO2, plan for high‑pressure components and relief routing.
- Digital and MRV
  - Deploy site‑level submetering and a central data platform to produce auditable energy, renewable, and refrigerant leakage data to SBTi standards; align with customer data requests.
- Supply chain
  - Long lead times for compressors/heat pumps, switchgear, transformers. Pre‑qualify OEMs/EPCs, framework agreements to lock pricing/slots.

6) Regulatory and market risk management (UK/EU relevant)
- F‑gas and PFAS/chemicals policy
  - EU and UK F‑gas phase‑downs mean 404A and many HFCs will be cost‑prohibitive or unobtainable. Avoid HFOs with PFAS concerns where possible; prioritise natural refrigerants to future‑proof.
- Carbon and electricity price volatility
  - Hedge via long‑term PPAs; retain optionality with staged procurement. Participate in flexibility markets to reduce non‑commodity charges exposure.
- Green claims scrutiny
  - Use additional, UK‑sited PPAs and avoid over‑reliance on unbundled REGOs. Aim for annual, moving to sub‑annual matching by 2030s to align with buyer expectations.
- Building regs and MEES
  - Any expansions/refurbs must meet rising efficiency standards; insulation upgrades help ensure compliance and reduce cooling load.
- Water and adiabatic
  - Tighten Legionella and water‑use management to mitigate regulatory risk and reputational concerns.

7) Governance, targets, and SBTi alignment
- Set near‑term 2030 target: e.g., ≥50% absolute Scope 1+2 reduction vs 2023 baseline, with milestones:
  - 2027: −20% energy intensity; 50% cut in HFC fugitive emissions; first 10 GWh/yr PPA live; 2–3 MWp PV installed.
  - 2030: 100% exit from 404A; ≥30% absolute electricity reduction vs baseline; ≥50% of electricity via additional renewables; 5–7 sites on natural refrigerants.
  - 2033: fleetwide natural refrigerants; ≥80% renewable electricity (additional); full electrification of heat and defrost.
  - 2035: net zero Scope 1+2 with minimal, high‑quality residuals.
- Link capex to abatement cost curve; report quarterly to customer on progress.

8) Quick wins to start this year
- Portfolio energy/refrigeration audit and metering plan; launch controls optimisation.
- HFC leak crackdown: fixed detection, maintenance regime, contract for refrigerant recovery.
- Procurement: start RFP for first PPA tranche; PV/BESS feasibility and roof surveys; DNO pre‑apps.
- Door/air‑seal upgrades, VSD retrofits, defrost optimisation.
- Standardise natural refrigerant specs and pre‑qualify suppliers.

Expected outcome
- By following this sequence, you can reduce electricity consumption by ~30–40%, eliminate high‑GWP refrigerants, cover residual use with additional renewables, and achieve net zero Scope 1+2 by 2035 within the £8–10m/yr capex envelope, while lowering opex, regulatory risk, and improving resilience and customer alignment.

Below is a pragmatic 2024–2030 pathway to achieve net zero Scope 1+2+3 under the CNDCP, sized to a 180 MW UK colo portfolio with ~220 ktCO2e/yr Scope 1+2 and c.£200m/year capex. It prioritises demand reduction, procurement decarbonisation, resilient onsite/near-site energy, diesel abatement, and supply-chain engagement, with clear sequencing and risk controls.

1) Baseline, targets, governance (2024–H1 2025)
- Update GHG inventory: location- and market-based Scope 2; separate construction vs operational emissions; tenant (downstream) electricity use; diesel test cycles; refrigerants; embodied carbon of capex (steel, cement, switchgear, batteries, gensets, IT fitout common areas); staff travel and waste. Align to GHG Protocol + CNDCP KPIs (renewable energy, water, circularity, energy efficiency).
- Set SBTi-aligned 2030 interim targets:
  - Scope 1+2: ≥90% absolute reduction vs 2020 baseline; residuals neutralised with durable removals by 2030.
  - Scope 3: ≥50% absolute or supplier coverage target (e.g., 67% suppliers by emissions with SBTs by 2028), with material-category targets (construction materials, purchased goods/services, capital goods, fuel/energy-related activities, downstream leased assets).
- Governance: Board-approved transition plan, internal carbon price (e.g., £150/t escalating to £300/t by 2030) applied to investment cases; capex ringfence for decarbonisation (40–50% of annual); link exec pay to CNDCP KPIs.

2) Energy efficiency and demand reduction (2024–2027)
Objective: Drive PUE toward 1.20 campus avg by 2027; reduce cooling energy and losses.
- Quick wins (2024–2025):
  - AI-enabled DCIM/EMS for dynamic setpoints; raise data hall temps to 24–27°C where SLAs allow; hot/cold aisle containment completion; VFD optimisation; UPS eco-mode where feasible.
  - Firmware and controls tuning of chillers/CRAC/CRAH; condenser water reset; free-cooling hours maximised; airflow management audits tenant-by-tenant.
  - Loss reduction: LV/MV transformer upgrades on replacement cycle; high-efficiency UPS (>97%).
- Medium measures (2025–2027):
  - Retrofit adiabatic/evaporative or hybrid coolers in Slough/Manchester, dry coolers for shoulder months, and heat-pump integration in West London.
  - White space fitout standards: blanking panels, perforated tile optimisation, CFD-led layout.
  - Metering granularity to rack/aisle; transparency portal for tenants with incentives.
Capex: ~£60–80m cumulative; energy savings 8–12% load; improves resilience and reduces renewables requirement.

3) Renewable electricity strategy and 24/7 coverage (2024–2030)
Objective: Move from annual REGO-matched grid to firm, additional, local/nearby supply with 24/7 time-matching by 2030, per CNDCP.
- Near-term (2024–2025):
  - Replace generic REGOs with long-term VPPA/CPPA for additional UK wind/solar (e.g., 500–700 GWh/yr initially; scale to full load). Prioritise GB wind for winter evenings and co-contract storage where pricing allows.
  - Begin 24/7 hourly matching pilots (e.g., Slough campus) using granular certification (EnergyTag, EACs) with suppliers like SSE, EDF, Statkraft, Google-style matching tools.
- Mid-term (2025–2028):
  - Multi-technology PPAs: onshore wind (Scotland), offshore wind tranche (CfD-aligned sleeved PPA), plus solar in Wales/England; target >110% annual coverage to account for curtailment and growth.
  - Procure 100–200 MW/200–400 MWh virtual or physical battery capacity via tolling/contracted flexibility to shape supply and reduce residual grid carbon at peak times.
  - Explore near-site private wire for Welsh campus: co-develop 150–200 MW wind/solar hybrid with 2–4 hours BESS; grid connection code compliance early.
- Long-term (2028–2030):
  - 24/7 matching portfolio completed: hourly residuals <5% backed by storage and green dispatchable options (biomethane CHP with CCS-ready design or green H2-ready turbines if available).
- KPIs: 100% renewable annually from 2025; 90–100% hourly matched by 2030.
Risks: PPA pricing volatility, grid constraints, curtailment; mitigate with diversified PPAs, step-in rights, and firming contracts.

4) Onsite/near-site energy and grid services (2025–2030)
- Onsite solar where roof/parking allows (limited, ~1–3% load). Prioritise Welsh site for larger ground-mount plus BESS.
- BESS at each campus (10–50 MW, 1–2 hours) for peak shaving, UPS ride-through, FFR/DSR revenue, and 24/7 matching; integrate with microgrid controls and islanding strategy.
- Thermal storage (ice/water) to shift cooling loads off-peak and align with renewable output.
- Explore waste heat recovery (Wales, West London): connect to district heating where viable; recoverable 5–20 MWth/site; secure offtake contracts to monetise and meet CNDCP circular criteria.

5) Diesel abatement and backup strategy (2024–2030)
Objective: Eliminate fossil diesel use and local air emissions while maintaining Tier III/IV resilience.
- Immediate (2024–2025):
  - Transition to HVO (EN 15940) for all test and emergency use; confirm OEM warranties, fuel stability and storage. This cuts Scope 1 by ~80–90% vs diesel and NOx/PM materially.
  - Optimise test regimes and load-bank sharing; capture and report runtime and fuel use granularly.
- Mid-term pilots (2025–2027):
  - Hydrogen-ready generators at Welsh site; start with HVO, plan conversion when green H2 supply firm. Pilot 1–2 MW fuel-cell UPS (SOFC/PEM) for critical blocks where feasible.
  - Hybrid backup: BESS + shorter runtime gensets to reduce starts; explore long-duration storage (LDES) as tech matures.
- 2028–2030:
  - Scale H2/gas engines or fuel cells if reliable green H2 supply and safety case approved; otherwise continue HVO + BESS with verified supply chain sustainability.
Regulatory watchouts: London air quality (NRMM), MCPD permits, local planning sensitivities; ensure SCR, particulate controls, and HVO certifications.

6) Refrigerants and leakage (2024–2028)
- Inventory all systems; transition from high-GWP HFCs to lower-GWP HFOs/CO2 across chiller refresh cycles.
- Leak detection, maintenance protocols, recovery/recycling contracts.
- Target refrigerant-related emissions near zero by 2028.

7) Construction and embodied carbon (Scope 3, capital goods) (2024–2030)
- Low-carbon design standards: whole-life carbon assessments (RICS), upfront carbon budgets (e.g., <500 kgCO2e/m2 for new build).
- Materials:
  - Cement: CEM III/LC3, GGBS/FA blends, alkali-activated binders where permitted.
  - Steel: EAF/recycled content; procure EPDs and require supplier SBTs by 2027.
  - Prefabrication/modular plant rooms to cut waste.
- MEP: specify SF6-free switchgear; high-efficiency transformers; circular procurement for racks/cables.
- Require contractors to meet PAS 2080; bid weighting for carbon; impose take-back schemes for IT fitout and batteries.

8) Supplier and tenant engagement (Scope 3, purchased goods and downstream leased assets)
- Supplier program (2024–2028):
