- Simplified method (prescriptive): Check glazing areas, orientation, aspect (single vs dual), and apply required shading/ventilation limits using ADO tables for London (high solar gain area).
- Dynamic thermal modelling: Use CIBSE TM59 (2017 or later) or an equivalent dynamic simulation to demonstrate overheating criteria are met, including purge ventilation and night-time conditions.

Key points and thresholds for the simplified method (London)
- High-risk category: London is classed as high risk in ADO.
- Single-aspect dwellings: South-facing single-aspect flats are generally not permissible via the simplified method unless strict limits are met; in many cases they fail and must go to dynamic modelling.
- Glazing area limits (indicative): For high-risk areas, single-aspect dwellings have very low allowable glazing ratios on the most exposed facade. If the glazing exceeds the tabled percentage of floor area (often around 13%–15% for single-aspect in high risk, lower for south/west), simplified compliance is not possible. Note: You must use the exact ADO Table 2.1/2.2 values for the façade orientation and dwelling type.
- Shading/solar control: Where simplified is used, either:
  - External shutters or shading with a minimum effective g-value (solar factor) per ADO, or
  - Low solar-gain glazing (e.g., g-value typically ≤0.4 for high-risk single-aspect) as specified in the ADO tables.
- Ventilation openings (minimum free area): Bedrooms and living spaces must achieve minimum free-area ventilation (e.g., ~13,000 mm² to 17,000 mm² per habitable room depending on dwelling type and risk band). Night-time purge (openable area) must meet ADO minimums; security-limited openings may not count unless proven.
- Noise/security constraints: If windows cannot be opened adequately due to noise, pollution, or security, simplified compliance often fails and modelling (with alternative measures like mechanical ventilation with summer bypass, or active cooling where permitted) is needed.

When it became mandatory
- Approved Document O applies to new residential buildings for applications submitted on or after 15 June 2022 (with transitional arrangements). It became effectively mandatory from 15 June 2022, with transitional provisions typically expiring for projects not commenced within one year.

Notes
- Many south-facing single-aspect flats in London fail the simplified route due to strict glazing and ventilation thresholds and therefore require TM59 dynamic modelling and/or design changes (reduced glazing, external shading, revised orientation, dual aspect, or controlled cooling where allowed).
- Always refer to the exact thresholds in the current ADO tables for glazing percentage, g-values, and minimum free-area ventilation, as they are prescriptive and vary by risk, orientation, and aspect.

Below is a concise summary of the requirements in Approved Document S (England) for a new residential building with parking. This assumes the development is within scope (England, Building Regulations Part S) and not subject to local planning policies that are more stringent.

Scope: New residential building with 50 flats and 60 parking spaces (on-site parking provided).

1) EV charging provision required
- Every new dwelling with an associated parking space must have an EV charge point.
- For residential buildings with communal or shared parking, provide:
  - At least 1 EV charge point per dwelling that has a parking space; and
  - Cable routes for all remaining parking spaces that do not get a charge point.

How this typically applies to blocks of flats:
- If each of the 50 flats has access to at least one of the 60 on‑site spaces (i.e., parking is provided for the dwellings), the development must install at least 50 charge points (one per dwelling) and provide cable routes to the remaining 10 spaces.
- If some flats are provided without any access to a parking space, those flats do not trigger a charge point, but all spaces serving the dwellings must be either fitted with charge points (to meet the one-per-dwelling rule where the dwelling has a space) or provided with cable routes.

Notes:
- “Cable routes” means ducting and draw ropes with adequate capacity for future installation of charge points and associated electrical/network cabling.
- Where a single charge point is intended to serve multiple dwellings (e.g., shared bays), the one-per-dwelling requirement still applies; in practice this means dedicated provision or an equivalent number of sockets/outlets.

2) Exemptions and relaxations
- Cost cap: If the total cost of installing charge points to meet the requirement exceeds £3,600 per required charge point (including design, equipment, installation, and grid connection apportioned), the number/specification can be reduced to remain within the cap. Any spaces not provided with a charge point due to the cap must have cable routes where reasonably practicable.
- Electrical capacity constraint: If the assessed maximum demand of the building (including the new EV load) would exceed the capacity of the local electricity connection (service head/transformer) and an upgrade is not feasible or would be disproportionately costly, the requirement can be reduced. Evidence of capacity limits from the DNO is expected. Where charge points are reduced, provide cable routes where practicable.
- Physical/practical constraints: If it is not technically feasible to install a charge point at a particular space (e.g., no safe mounting location, heritage or structural constraints), provide cable routes where practicable and document the constraint.
- Major renovations: Different triggers apply; for new buildings the above applies in full. (Your scheme is a new build.)

3) Minimum charge-point specification
- Power rating: Minimum 7 kW AC nominal output per charge point (Mode 3).
- Socket/connector: Type 2 socket outlet (EN 62196-2) or tethered Type 2 lead.
- Smart functionality: Must be smart/connected and capable of:
  - Demand-side response and load management (including randomised delay, scheduling).
  - Measuring/recording electricity consumption and communicating data.
  - Remote firmware/security updates.
- Safety and standards: Must comply with:
  - BS EN 61851 series (electric vehicle conductive charging systems).
  - BS EN 62196 series (plugs, socket-outlets, vehicle connectors).
  - Electrical installation to BS 7671 (IET Wiring Regulations), including RCD protection and PME earthing mitigation where required (e.g., open-PEN protection).
- Accessibility and usability: Installed to be accessible, safely located, and appropriately labelled; weatherproof to suitable IP rating; with adequate protection against impact where relevant.
- Metering: Capable of recording energy delivered; MID-approved metering where used for billing.
- Load management for multiple points: If multiple charge points are on a shared supply, include an active load management system to keep total EV load within the building’s agreed supply capacity.

Practical application to your scheme (typical case)
- Provide at least 50 x 7 kW Type 2 smart charge points serving the dwellings.
- Provide cable routes to the remaining 10 spaces.
- If cost/capacity constraints prevent full provision, document the assessment, install as many as permissible within the cap/capacity, and provide cable routes to the rest.

Always confirm with:
- The latest Approved Document S and any updates.
- Local planning policies (some authorities require more provision or higher specs).
- DNO capacity and any required connection upgrades.
- Any site-specific constraints (e.g., listed building elements).

Here’s what applies in England under Approved Document F, Volume 1: Dwellings (2021 edition with 2022 amendments) for a new airtight dwelling with MVHR (mechanical ventilation with heat recovery) targeting an envelope airtightness of 3 m³/(h·m²) at 50 Pa.

Whole‑dwelling ventilation rate (continuous supply and extract, System 4 MVHR)
- Minimum whole‑dwelling ventilation rate: the greater of:
  1) Sum of minimum extract rates from all “wet” rooms (kitchen, bathrooms, WCs, utility), plus
  2) A rate based on the total number of bedrooms (and an occupancy allowance), typically expressed as:
     - 1 bedroom: 13 l/s
     - 2 bedrooms: 17 l/s
     - 3 bedrooms: 21 l/s
     - 4 bedrooms: 25 l/s
     - 5 bedrooms: 29 l/s
     - Add 4 l/s for each additional bedroom over five
- Minimum continuous extract rates per room (typical AD F values):
  - Kitchen: 13 l/s
  - Utility: 8 l/s
  - Bathroom: 8 l/s
  - En‑suite: 6 l/s
  - WC: 6 l/s
- Minimum continuous supply to “habitable rooms” (living rooms, bedrooms) is then set so that total supply equals the whole‑dwelling rate, with distribution meeting room‑level minimums given in the guidance.
- Boost rates: MVHR must be capable of providing boost (higher extract rates) meeting intermittent extract equivalents in wet rooms (e.g., kitchen 30 l/s adjacent to hob or 60 l/s elsewhere; bathroom 15 l/s; WC 6 l/s), typically via humidity, CO₂, occupancy, or manual control. Systems must be designed to avoid noise leading to user disablement.

Commissioning and testing requirements
- Airtightness testing:
  - Mandatory for new dwellings. Your target is 3 m³/(h·m²) at 50 Pa; test and report per Approved Document L/Part L procedures (notified in the BREL report and EPC).
- Ventilation system testing and commissioning:
  - All terminals (supply and extract) must be measured on site for actual airflow in normal (trickle) and boost settings, using calibrated instruments and recognized methods (e.g., flow hood).
  - Commission the system to meet or exceed the minimum whole‑dwelling rate and room‑level rates and to achieve balanced supply and extract (net imbalance typically not exceeding 10% unless justified).
  - Specific fan power and noise should be checked against design/manufacturer data; filters installed and documented.
  - Provide a compliant commissioning notice and test report (airflow results per room, settings, instrument calibration) to Building Control and the homeowner, using the AD F commissioning sheet.
  - Where acoustic constraints prevent achieving boost rates, document the justification and any compensatory measures.
- Installation and labelling:
  - Provide access for maintenance (filters/heat exchanger), label controls, and set default/holiday modes as per guidance.
  - Provide user information (O&M manual) covering operation, filter changes, and maintenance schedule.

Indoor air quality monitoring requirement
- CO₂ monitoring in the principal living space is required in new dwellings with continuous mechanical supply (including MVHR).
  - Provide a fixed, mains‑powered CO₂ monitor with a display visible to occupants, located in the principal habitable room.
  - The monitor should:
    - Indicate concentration bands (e.g., green/amber/red) or actual ppm.
    - Provide alerts when CO₂ exceeds 1,500 ppm for a set period and guidance to increase ventilation (e.g., boost, open windows).
    - Have data‑logging or trend capability recommended but not explicitly mandated.
  - Portable/battery devices are generally not accepted as the sole solution; follow AD F stipulations for fixed monitors.
- For bedrooms, AD F encourages (but does not mandate) CO₂ monitoring; however, ensure MVHR provides adequate nighttime ventilation rates to meet IAQ targets.

Notes and practical tips
- Given the low airtightness (3 m³/(h·m²)), infiltration credit is minimal; do not rely on it in sizing. Size and set the MVHR to fully meet whole‑dwelling rates.
- Ensure background ventilators (trickle vents) are not required when a properly designed MVHR is installed; AD F does not require background ventilators with continuous mechanical supply and extract unless part of a mixed system.
- Keep design documentation: schedules of design rates, duct sizing, pressure drops, fan duty, noise calculations, and balancing provisions.

If you share the dwelling’s room schedule and bedroom count, I can calculate the exact whole‑dwelling and room distribution rates per AD F tables and produce a commissioning checklist template.

Transitional provision (England, Building Regulations Part L uplift 2021):
- If a “relevant application” (full plans, initial notice, or building notice) was submitted before 15 June 2022, the work may proceed under the previous energy efficiency standards (Part L 2013), but only if work on that specific building is “started” before 15 June 2023.
- “Start of work” is defined narrowly. For new dwellings, excavation for foundations, pouring of concrete for foundations, trench or pad foundations, or piling and casting of a ground beam generally count. Site strip, fencing, demolition, or service diversions do not.

Consequence if the start-of-work test fails:
- If work to that dwelling did not start by 15 June 2023, the transitional protection is lost. The dwelling must comply with the current requirements introduced by the 2021 uplift (Part L 2021 and associated Approved Document L 2021), including the new notional dwelling, primary energy target, fabric/airtightness standards, and associated SAP 10.2 methodology.
- Foundations started on 1 August 2024 are well after 15 June 2023, so the project no longer benefits from the transition and must be designed, assessed, and inspected to Part L 2021.

- What Gateway 1 requires:
  - Submission of a Fire Statement that demonstrates fire safety has been considered in the land-use planning stage (site layout, access for fire and rescue, water supplies for firefighting, means of escape, external wall materials/risks, fire spread, evacuation strategy, etc.).
  - It forms part of a Fire Safety Information requirement to support planning decisions for relevant buildings.
  - The planning authority must take fire safety matters into account when determining the application.

- When it applies:
  - At the planning application stage (prior approval/full planning) for “relevant buildings.”
  - A building is “relevant” if it is at least 18m in height or 7 or more storeys and contains two or more residential units. Your proposed 9-storey, 32 m residential block qualifies, so Gateway 1 applies at submission of the planning application.

- Statutory consultee:
  - The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) as the statutory consultee on fire safety for relevant planning applications under Gateway 1.

- What is required: The Principal Accountable Person (PAP) must prepare and maintain a Safety Case and produce a Safety Case Report. The report must:
  - Identify the building’s major fire and structural hazards
  - Explain the risk assessments and safety management systems in place
  - Demonstrate how risks are being reduced so far as is reasonably practicable (SFAIRP)
  - Set out control measures, inspection/maintenance regimes, resident engagement, emergency arrangements, and how the PAP monitors, audits, and reviews performance
  - Be kept up to date and available to the Building Safety Regulator (BSR) on request, and submitted as part of the application for a Building Assessment Certificate when invited by the BSR

- When it must be produced:
  - The building is a “higher-risk building” (HRB) in occupation (at least 7 storeys or 18 m and contains at least 2 residential units). For occupied HRBs:
    - Registration: All occupied HRBs in England had to be registered with the BSR by 1 October 2023. For any newly becoming-occupied HRB, registration must be completed before occupation.
    - Safety Case and Safety Case Report: The PAP must have the Safety Case prepared and be able to provide the Safety Case Report to the BSR when requested. Practically, the PAP should have it ready now and will need to submit it when the BSR invites an application for a Building Assessment Certificate. There is no fixed calendar deadline to submit the report unless and until the BSR requests it, but it must be maintained continuously and reflect current building risks and controls.

- Penalties for failing to register or comply:
  - Failure to register an occupied HRB by the required time, or permitting occupation of an unregistered HRB: a criminal offence. Penalties can include unlimited fines and/or imprisonment (up to 2 years for certain offences). The BSR can also issue compliance notices and prohibition notices.
  - Failure to comply with ongoing PAP duties (e.g., to assess and manage building safety risks, keep a Safety Case, produce a Safety Case Report when required, maintain a residents’ engagement strategy, complaints system, mandatory occurrence reporting, provide information to the BSR): criminal offences. Penalties include unlimited fines and/or imprisonment (for individuals responsible) and enforcement action such as compliance or contravention notices; failure to comply with such notices can also attract criminal sanctions.
  - Corporate and individual liability can apply; directors/managers can be prosecuted where offences are committed with their consent, connivance, or attributable to their neglect.

Note: The building is in Manchester (England), so the above applies under the Building Safety Act 2022 and associated regulations, including the Higher-Risk Buildings (Management of Safety Risks etc) (England) Regulations 2023 and Registration of Higher-Risk Buildings Regulations 2023.

- Competence to demonstrate
  - Organisational and individual competence to plan, manage, and monitor design work so that it complies with the Building Regulations, including Part B (fire) and Part A (structure), and that foreseeable building safety risks are eliminated, reduced, or controlled.
  - Ability to coordinate design work across all designers and ensure that design information is sufficient, timely, and properly communicated to the Principal Contractor and other dutyholders.
  - Capability to identify when specialist competence is needed (e.g., fire engineering, structural engineering) and to procure/coordinate it.
  - Suitable governance, resources, skills, knowledge, experience, and behaviours (SKEB) proportionate to an HRB’s complexity, including robust change control and assurance of design compliance through gateways.
  - Understanding of the Building Safety Act 2022 regime, Higher-Risk Building (HRB) definitions, the Gateway process (especially Gateway 2 design-as-built assurance), golden thread information management, and mandatory occurrence reporting.

- Standard underpinning the assessment
  - The competence assessment is expected to be underpinned by PAS 8671 (Principal Designer competence) within the PAS 8670 series (which sets the overarching framework for built environment competence). PAS 8671 builds on PAS 8670 and aligns with BSI Flex 8670 principles. Many assessment schemes (e.g., RIBA, CIOB, ICE, etc.) map to PAS 8671 for Principal Designer (Building Regulations) competence.

- Personal liability risk
  - The Principal Designer under the Building Regulations dutyholder regime is an individual dutyholder (even when appointed via an organisation). Failure to fulfil duties can lead to personal criminal liability, including:
    - Investigation and potential prosecution by a Building Control Authority or the Building Safety Regulator.
    - Criminal offences for breaches of the Building Regulations and dutyholder requirements, with unlimited fines and, for more serious or persistent breaches, the possibility of imprisonment.
    - Liability can attach to senior individuals (“consent, connivance, or neglect”) as well as to the corporate body.
  - Civil exposure also exists (negligence, breach of contract), but the regime primarily creates criminal enforcement risk for non-compliance. Professional indemnity insurance may not cover criminal penalties, so robust competence and governance are critical.

Here’s the position for higher-risk buildings (HRBs) in England that started under the old building control regime before 1 October 2023.

Transitional provisions
- Projects that had “sufficiently progressed” under the old regime by 1 October 2023 can continue under their existing building control body (local authority or approved inspector) and do not have to come under the Building Safety Regulator (BSR) mid‑project, provided they remain continuously “sufficiently progressed.”
- For HRBs, “sufficiently progressed” meant the works had reached the defined stage by the transition cut-off and then met a further evidence deadline in spring 2024 (see below).

Cut‑off date(s)
- 1 October 2023: Start of the new regime and the relevant transition cut‑off.
- 6 April 2024: Deadline to submit the required transitional notifications/evidence (e.g., that work had sufficiently progressed by 1 October 2023 and that a valid initial notice or plans approval was in place) to remain under the old regime.

If both were satisfied, the project could continue with its original building control pathway and not move to BSR oversight mid‑construction.

What triggers a forced transition to BSR oversight
- Failure to meet transitional tests or deadlines:
  - If the project had not “sufficiently progressed” by 1 October 2023; or
  - If the necessary transitional submissions/evidence were not provided by 6 April 2024; then the project must transition to BSR oversight.
- Material changes that break continuity:
  - Lapsing/withdrawal/cancellation of the initial notice or approval, or a change of building control body that cannot be maintained under transitional rules.
  - Substantial design or scope changes that amount to a new controlled works package requiring fresh approval under the new regime.
- Commencing a new work package after the transition:
  - If new, separate controlled works for the HRB commence that were not covered by the original transitional approval, those works fall under BSR (Gateway 2 etc.).
- Significant pause or cessation that invalidates the “continuous progression” assumption (e.g., where commencement markers are not maintained and a fresh approval would be needed).

Practical pointer
- If your HRB project demonstrably commenced/sufficiently progressed before 1 Oct 2023 and you lodged the required transitional evidence by 6 Apr 2024—and you have maintained the same control route without lapses—you can generally remain under the old regime. Any break in that chain or new works will trigger BSR oversight.

Here’s a clear summary tailored to Higher-Risk Buildings (HRBs) under the Building Safety Act 2022 and associated regulations in England.

What ‘golden thread’ information must be maintained
The golden thread is the up-to-date, accurate, digital record of information needed to understand a building and keep it safe throughout design, construction, and occupation. For HRBs, it must at minimum cover:

- Building description and key details:
  - Location, storeys, height, use, fire/smoke control features, structural system, materials known to affect safety (e.g., cladding, insulation), compartmentation strategy.
  - As-constructed drawings and models (where applicable), including fire and structural safety-critical details.

- Design and construction information:
  - Current and historic versions of design intent and as-built information for fire and structural safety.
  - Specifications of safety-critical products and systems, approvals, change control records (Gateways 2 and 3 change records), deviations and justifications.
  - Competence declarations for dutyholders and key designers/contractors.

- Building safety risk assessments and strategies:
  - Fire strategy (final), structural safety basis, smoke control strategy, evacuation plan/strategy, resident profile assumptions (where relevant to safety measures).
  - The Safety Case and Safety Case Report inputs (hazards, risk assessments, control measures, ALARP demonstrations).

- Testing, commissioning, and assurance:
  - Certificates, test reports, commissioning records for life safety systems (e.g., fire detection and alarm, sprinklers, smoke control, AOVs, emergency lighting, firefighting lifts), fire doors, cavity barriers, structural elements.
  - Digital O&M data, manufacturer instructions, warranties, inspection/maintenance regimes, access/maintenance strategies for safety systems.

- Change control and decisions:
  - Record of notifiable/major changes, BSR notifications/approvals, rationale and risk assessments for changes affecting building safety.

- Construction Control Plan and Building Control records (Gateway 2/3):
  - Construction control plan, competence plan, inspection/test plans, records of site audits, non-conformance, remedial actions, and the Principal Designer/Principal Contractor declarations at Gateway 3.
  - Building control correspondence, conditions, certificates, and compliance evidence.

- Resident engagement and complaints (for occupation phase):
  - Resident engagement strategy and key communications about building safety.
  - Significant complaints or issues that relate to building safety risks and how they were addressed.

- Emergency arrangements:
  - Fire and emergency file, emergency information pack for Fire and Rescue Service (e.g., Premises Information Box content), plans for disabled residents (where applicable), firefighting facilities and access.

- Registration and dutyholder info:
  - HRB registration details, identity and contact details of the Accountable Person(s) and Principal Accountable Person (PAP) on completion/occupation; roles and responsibilities.

Format requirements
- Digital by default:
  - Must be created, stored, and maintained in a digital, secure, and retrievable format. Paper alone is not sufficient.
- Structured, accessible, and version-controlled:
  - Information should be indexed, searchable, and auditable, with change history and who approved changes.
  - Use common data environments (CDE) or an equivalent secure system with role-based access.
- Interoperable/open where practicable:
  - Use open, machine-readable formats where possible (e.g., IFC for models, PDF/A for documents, CSV/JSON for data schedules). Ensure metadata, revision, and status codes are clear.
- Accurate and current:
  - Keep the as-built baseline current at Gateway 3 and maintain updates during occupation as changes occur.
- Proportionate:
  - Level of detail should be sufficient to operate and maintain the building safely; focus on fire and structural safety-critical information.

When handover obligations to the Principal Accountable Person are triggered
- At completion/transition to occupation:
  - The Principal Contractor and Principal Designer must provide prescribed information to enable the PAP to manage building safety risks on completion of building work (Gateway 3).
  - Handover is triggered when building work on an HRB is complete and before occupation, aligned with:
    - Application for Building Control completion certificate to the Building Safety Regulator (BSR), and
    - The HRB registration and certification processes required prior to occupation.

- Specifically, handover must include the prescribed “golden thread” information necessary for:
  - The PAP to prepare/maintain the Safety Case, Safety Case Report, resident engagement strategy, and mandatory occurrence reporting arrangements.
  - Ongoing operation, inspection, testing, and maintenance of all safety systems.

- Practical markers you can use:
  - Gateway 3 submission: Provide the as-built information, compliance declarations, and evidence pack to the BSR. In parallel, prepare the digital handover set for the PAP.
  - Prior to occupation: PAP cannot lawfully permit occupation of a new HRB until it is registered and the building control completion certificate is issued. The PAP needs the golden thread package in time to discharge their occupation-phase duties from day 1.

Who is responsible when
- During design and construction: Client must ensure arrangements are in place for creating and maintaining the golden thread. Principal Designer and Principal Contractor must gather, verify, and manage it, and produce the prescribed information at Gateway 3.
- On completion/occupation: The PAP becomes responsible for maintaining the golden thread throughout occupation, updating it for any safety-related changes and keeping it available for the BSR.

Practical deliverables checklist for handover to the PAP
- Final as-built drawings/models with change logs and compliance evidence
- Fire strategy (final), structural design summary, and safety-critical product schedules
- Commissioning and certification pack for life-safety and structural elements
- O&M manuals (digital), manufacturers’ data, maintenance plans, asset register
- Construction Control Plan records, Gateway 2/3 change control and approvals
- Principal Designer and Principal Contractor compliance declarations
- Building Control/BSR correspondence and completion certificate application pack
- Resident engagement strategy template/inputs and emergency information set
- Information governance: index, metadata, access controls, versioning, update protocols

If you tell me your project’s stage and whether it’s new build, conversion, or refurbishment of an existing HRB, I can tailor a project-specific golden thread contents list and a handover timeline.

Short answer: Yes, SECR applies, and the company must disclose energy use and greenhouse gas emissions in its Directors’ Report (or Energy & Carbon Report) in the annual accounts.

Details:

1) Do SECR rules apply?
- SECR (Streamlined Energy and Carbon Reporting) applies to:
  - All quoted companies; and
  - Large unquoted companies and large LLPs that meet at least two of the following:
    • ≥250 employees
    • Turnover > £36 million
    • Balance sheet total > £18 million
- Your company (UK-incorporated, 280 employees, £55m turnover, £40m balance sheet) meets all three “large” thresholds, so SECR applies.

2) What must be reported (disclosure scope)?
For large unquoted companies:
- Energy use:
  - UK energy consumption in kWh from:
    • Electricity
    • Gas
    • Transport (e.g., fuel used in company-owned/leased vehicles; business travel in rental cars/grey fleet if you choose to include)
- Greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions:
  - Total gross Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions (tonnes CO2e) from the above energy use
  - Scope 3 is not mandatory, but if you include material elements (e.g., transmission & distribution, well-to-tank, business travel), state what’s included
- Intensity ratio:
  - At least one emissions intensity metric relevant to the business (e.g., tCO2e per £m turnover; for property portfolios, also commonly tCO2e per m² NLA or per building)
- Methodologies:
  - Describe methodologies, factors, and standards used (e.g., DEFRA/BEIS emission factors; GHG Protocol; how estimates and boundaries were set)
- Energy efficiency actions:
  - A brief narrative of principal energy efficiency actions taken during the financial year
- Comparatives:
  - Present at least one year of prior figures once you are in your second reporting year; explain any material changes in methodology or boundaries
- Exemptions/omissions:
  - If obtaining the information is impracticable, or if disclosure would be seriously prejudicial to interests, you may omit with a clear explanation
  - You may exclude de minimis energy/EM (but explain basis)

3) Where must disclosures be made?
- In the Directors’ Report within the company’s annual report and accounts (often titled the “Energy and Carbon Report” section)
- Also file with Companies House along with the annual accounts
- If part of a group, the parent can report at group level covering subsidiaries’ UK energy/emissions; subsidiaries may cross‑refer if fully covered

Practical notes for a commercial property portfolio:
- Clarify operational control boundaries for landlord vs. tenant energy
- Separately track:
  - Landlord-purchased electricity and gas for common areas and central plant
  - Company fleet fuel and reimbursed business mileage (if included)
- Choose at least one sector‑relevant intensity metric (e.g., tCO2e/m², tCO2e/£m rent)
- Use current UK Government GHG conversion factors for the reporting year and disclose location‑based vs market‑based figures if you use green tariffs/REGO-backed electricity (market-based is optional but good practice; location-based is standard for SECR)

Conclusion: The company is in scope as a large unquoted company. It must disclose UK energy consumption, Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions, at least one intensity ratio, methodologies, and a summary of energy efficiency actions, within the Directors’ Report in the annual accounts filed with Companies House.

Short answer
- In scope? Yes. The UK parent is in scope of CSRD via its EU subsidiaries because the group has a significant EU presence through German subsidiaries that together exceed the €150m EU net turnover threshold and have a large footprint in an EU member state.
- First reporting year: FY 2028 (report published in 2029) under the “non‑EU parent with large EU activity” route.
- Assurance: Limited assurance over sustainability reporting initially; likely to move to reasonable assurance at a later mandated date.

Detail and reasoning
- Route to scope: A non‑EU (UK) parent becomes subject to CSRD at the consolidated (global) level if:
  1) It has EU net turnover > €150m for each of the last two consecutive financial years; and
  2) It has in the EU either (a) a large subsidiary or (b) a small/medium subsidiary listed on an EU regulated market or (c) a branch with net turnover > €40m.
- Your facts: Two German subsidiaries, c. 300 employees each (so at least one will likely be “large”: >250 employees), and combined EU turnover €180m. That satisfies the EU turnover threshold and the presence of at least one large EU subsidiary. Therefore the UK parent is in scope via Article 40a CSRD (the “third‑country parent” provision).

Timing
- First financial year to report: FY starting on or after 1 January 2028.
- Publication deadline: 12 months after year‑end (Member States may set earlier, but CSRD allows 12 months) — so for a 31 Dec 2028 year‑end, report due by 31 Dec 2029.
- Note: If any German subsidiary itself meets “large” criteria, it will have its own CSRD obligations earlier (FY 2025 for large PIE >500 employees; FY 2026 for other large EU undertakings), unless it can rely on a qualifying parent consolidated ESRS report that covers it. Given your parent is non‑EU and not reporting before 2028, each German sub may need to report locally from FY 2026 unless an exemption applies and a compliant equivalent report is provided.

Assurance
- For the third‑country parent report (Article 40a): limited assurance required initially over the sustainability reporting (and over the EU‑turnover‑only scoping assessment). The auditor must be an EU statutory auditor or another independent assurance services provider allowed under national law; if the report is prepared under equivalent standards outside the EU, it must still obtain limited assurance acceptable in the Member State where the largest EU subsidiary or branch is located (Germany).
- The CSRD foresees a later move from limited to reasonable assurance, expected after the Commission adopts assurance standards and a transition period (indicatively no earlier than reports published for FY 2028/2029+; Member State transposition will confirm timing). Current expectation: limited assurance for the first years, with reasonable assurance phased in thereafter.

Practical next steps
- Confirm EU turnover > €150m for each of the last two consecutive years.
- Identify which German entity is the “most significant” for filing location; Germany will likely require the Article 40a report to be filed in Germany.
- Plan for subsidiary‑level CSRD from FY 2026 if they are large, unless a compliant consolidated report covering them is available and accepted as an exemption.
- Begin ESRS‑aligned double materiality assessment and data gap analysis; line up an assurance provider for limited assurance.

Here’s the current position and what a UK Main Market premium-listed company should plan for:

Status of UK Sustainability Reporting Standards (UK SRS)
- The UK government confirmed it will create UK-endorsed versions of IFRS S1 and IFRS S2 (to be called UK SRS S1 and UK SRS S2), with possible limited UK-specific modifications.
- The UK Endorsement Board (UKEB) consulted on endorsement in 2024/2025 and is progressing toward final UK SRS.
- FCA plans to align listed-company climate and broader sustainability disclosure rules with UK SRS, replacing TCFD-based rules over time.

Expected timing
- Target applicability: financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2026 for listed companies, subject to final FCA consultation and rulemaking.
- Transition: The FCA has indicated a phased approach—initially climate (UK SRS S2) with core S1 elements to enable connectivity/baseline disclosures, then broader S1 requirements maturing over time.
- Until new rules take effect, existing TCFD-based Listing Rule (LR 9.8.6R(8)) and FCA ESG Sourcebook rules continue to apply.

What the company should do now (for FY2025 and readiness)
- Continue to disclose against TCFD for FY2025 in line with current FCA rules.
- Start preparing to report under UK SRS (IFRS S1/S2 aligned) from FY2026:
  - Gap assess TCFD vs IFRS S2/UK SRS S2 and the cross-cutting/general requirements in S1 (e.g., governance, strategy, risk management, metrics/targets, financial statement connectivity, materiality definition, industry-based metrics).
  - Plan for scenario analysis and financed/Scope 3 methodologies consistent with IFRS S2 (including use of GHG Protocol), and for more granular transition plans and risk/opportunity quantification.
  - Strengthen data, controls, and assurance readiness: UK policy signals point toward limited assurance on sustainability information over time; build internal controls and evidence trails now.
  - Consider location of disclosures: UK SRS will generally expect disclosures in the annual report (management report) with cross-references; check FCA proposals on placement and digital tagging.
  - Monitor FCA/UKEB publications in 2025–2026 for final endorsement decisions, FCA consultation, and effective dates, including any transitional reliefs (e.g., Scope 3, scenario analysis depth, comparative information).

Practical next steps
- Commission a formal S1/S2 readiness assessment in H2 2025.
- Map current TCFD content to IFRS S2 topics and SASB/industry metrics; identify data owners and gaps (especially Scope 3 categories, climate resilience, and financial effects disclosures).
- Engage audit committee on governance, internal controls, and potential assurance scope/timing.
- Prepare to include comparative information and consider digital reporting/taxonomy developments once mandated.

In short: keep reporting under TCFD for FY2025, and get ready to transition to UK SRS (aligned to IFRS S1/S2) likely from FY2026, subject to FCA’s final rules.

Here’s what changed for ESOS Phase 3 after the original 5 December 2023 deadline, and what you still need to do after submitting your compliance notification in June 2024.

What new/remaining Phase 3 obligations applied after December 2023
- Use of an energy intensity metric: Participants must calculate and report at least one energy intensity metric (e.g., kWh per full-time equivalent, per square metre, per unit of output) for their significant energy consumption.
- Additional data disclosure: Provide more detail in the notification and ESOS report (e.g., how total energy consumption was calculated, breakdown of energy use, estimations used).
- De minimis threshold reduction: The allowable “de minimis” proportion of total energy that can be excluded from audits/coverage reduced from 10% to 5%.
- Stronger audit and reporting standards: ESOS energy audits must align with relevant standards (e.g., BS EN 16247) and include more robust opportunity assessments with estimated savings and costs.
- Director-level accountability: A board‑level director must review and sign off the ESOS assessment report.
- Public disclosure (if asked): Certain summary information may need to be shared publicly if requested by the scheme administrator.
- Requirement to set a metric-based target or action plan: New for Phase 3, participants must set either a:
  - Net zero target, or
  - Energy efficiency/consumption/greenhouse gas reduction target,
  and/or produce an ESOS energy efficiency action plan that responds to audit findings.

Action plan and target requirements and deadlines
- What you must do:
  - Either set an energy or emissions reduction target and/or develop an ESOS energy efficiency action plan covering your significant energy use. The plan should translate identified opportunities into actions, with timelines, responsibilities, estimated savings, and monitoring metrics.
  - Include at least one energy intensity metric and baseline.
  - Obtain director sign‑off for the target/action plan.

- Deadline to put in place:
  - Action plan/target must be set no later than 6 months after your Phase 3 compliance notification date.
  - For a group that notified compliance in June 2024, the action plan/target deadline is 6 months from your actual submission date (e.g., submitted 5 June 2024 → deadline 5 December 2024).

- Annual reporting on progress:
  - You must report progress annually against the target/action plan and energy intensity metric.
  - First annual progress update is due 12 months after the action plan/target deadline (i.e., roughly by December 2025 if you submitted June 2024), and then annually thereafter for the Phase 3 compliance period.

Practical next steps
- Confirm your compliance notification date to fix the exact 6‑month deadline.
- Compile an action plan aligned to ESOS audit findings, with costs, savings, paybacks, owners, and timelines.
- Select and document at least one energy intensity metric and a baseline year.
- Get director approval and retain evidence for potential audit.
- Set up a process to collect data and produce the first annual progress report by the 12‑month mark after the action plan deadline.

Short answer
Yes. The company falls within scope of the UK Companies (Strategic Report) (Climate-related Financial Disclosure) Regulations 2022, so it must include TCFD-aligned climate disclosures in its Strategic Report (or Energy and Carbon Report section, as applicable) in its annual report.

Scope test
The 2022 Regulations apply to:
- UK companies that are “traded,” banking or insurance companies; and
- Large UK companies that are not in those categories but have more than 500 employees and are “high turnover” (over £500m).

Your company:
- Private (not listed) but UK-registered.
- 600 employees (≥500).
- £700m turnover (>£500m).
Therefore it is an “in‑scope” large company and must make the required climate-related financial disclosures.

What must be disclosed (TCFD‑aligned)
Disclose, to the extent necessary for an understanding of the company’s business and its development, performance and position, and the impacts of the company’s operations, the following, aligned to the four TCFD pillars:

1) Governance
- The governance arrangements in relation to assessing and managing climate-related risks and opportunities.
- Who (board/committee/management) is responsible and how oversight is exercised.

2) Strategy
- How climate-related risks and opportunities are identified over the short, medium and long term.
- The actual and potential impacts of climate-related risks and opportunities on the business model and strategy.
- How these are integrated into business planning and financial planning.
- A description of any climate-related scenario analysis performed (including at least qualitative analysis; quantitative where practicable), and how resilient the strategy is to climate-related scenarios.

3) Risk management
- How climate-related risks are identified, assessed and managed.
- How these processes are integrated into the company’s overall risk management framework.

4) Metrics and targets
- The key climate-related performance indicators used to assess progress (including at least Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions; Scope 3 where material and data is available or can be obtained at proportionate cost).
- The targets set to manage climate-related risks and opportunities, and performance against those targets.
- The intensity ratios used (e.g., tCO2e per £m revenue) where appropriate.
- Methodologies, standards and boundaries used for GHG calculations, and any changes year-on-year.

Materiality and proportionality
- Disclose “to the extent necessary” for understanding; if you conclude any required item is not relevant, you must state that and explain why.
- Scenario analysis and Scope 3: qualitative and proportionate approaches are acceptable where quantitative analysis/data is not yet practicable, but you should explain limitations and plans to improve.

Location of disclosures
- Include these disclosures in the Strategic Report of the company’s annual report.
- If you prepare a Group Strategic Report, make group-level disclosures there. Subsidiary-level disclosures may be cross‑referred where permitted.
- If any information is placed elsewhere in the annual report (e.g., a separate sustainability section), the Strategic Report should contain a clear cross‑reference. Purely web-only disclosures do not satisfy the requirement; you may cross‑refer to the Directors’ Report or Non‑Financial and Sustainability Information Statement if used, but ensure they are within the same annual report.

Related requirements to remember
- SECR (Streamlined Energy and Carbon Reporting) still applies if you meet its thresholds; those energy and carbon figures typically appear in the Directors’ Report or Strategic Report. Avoid duplication and ensure consistency with the TCFD metrics.
- Narrative must cover the financial year; include comparative information where relevant and explain any restatements or methodology changes.

Practical next steps
- Confirm group vs parent-only scope and whether consolidated disclosures are needed.
- Map existing SECR/GHG processes to TCFD metrics/targets.
- Document board oversight and management responsibilities.
- Perform proportionate scenario analysis and define short/medium/long-term horizons.
- Determine material Scope 3 categories and a plan to improve data quality over time.

References
- Companies (Strategic Report) (Climate-related Financial Disclosure) Regulations 2022 (SI 2022/31), effective for periods starting on/after 6 April 2022.
- BEIS/Department for Business and Trade guidance on climate-related financial disclosure (TCFD-aligned) for in-scope UK companies.

- Is the existing EPC valid for the letting? No. An EPC is valid for 10 years. An EPC dated 15 March 2015 expired on 14 March 2025, so it will not be valid for a letting on 1 July 2026. A new EPC must be obtained before marketing/granting the lease.

  - Letting in breach of the MEES prohibition (i.e., letting a sub‑standard property) where the breach lasts:

    - 3 months or more: up to the greater of £10,000 or 20% of the rateable value (capped at £150,000).

Notes:

Exemption: “Seven‑year payback” (cost‑effectiveness) exemption for non‑domestic PRS. It applies where all relevant energy‑efficiency improvements that are qualifying measures are not cost‑effective because none would pay back through energy savings within seven years.

Duration: 5 years from the date of registration (unless the property is sold/let changes trigger earlier re‑assessment).

Evidence to upload to the PRS Exemptions Register:
- A recommendation report identifying relevant improvements (e.g., EPC recommendation report, or a report by a qualified surveyor/energy assessor).
- A detailed seven‑year payback calculation showing that the cheapest qualifying measure fails the 7‑year simple payback test (and, if assessed, that all relevant measures fail). This should include:
  - Measure description(s)
  - Installed cost quotes or cost estimates from a qualified installer/supplier
  - Assumed annual energy savings (kWh) and cost savings (£), with sources/assumptions
  - Energy price(s) used and date
  - Calculation method and result demonstrating payback > 7 years
- Evidence of quotes: at least one, and usually expected two or more, written quotations or a formal costed proposal for the measure(s) from reputable installers/suppliers.
- The current EPC (showing band F) and property details.
- Landlord declaration confirming the information is true and that the measures have been considered and are not cost‑effective under the MEES seven‑year test.

Note: If the landlord has assessed all relevant measures and none meet the seven‑year payback, include that statement and supporting calculations for each. The exemption must be reviewed and re‑registered (with updated evidence) when it expires or if circumstances change (e.g., energy prices, new measures).

Here’s a concise overview for a non-domestic property in Scotland:

Key differences: Scotland vs England & Wales (E&W)
- EPC format and validity:
  - Both require EPCs on sale/let; both last 10 years.
  - Scotland uses its own EPC register (Scottish EPC Register) and SBEM/DSM under Scottish Building Regulations. EPCs display an asset rating and include a separate Recommendations Report.
  - E&W uses the England & Wales register.
- Triggering extra duties:
  - Scotland has Section 63 duties for larger buildings (see below).
  - E&W does not have Section 63; instead, it has MEES (minimum EPC E, tightening to C/B in future).
- Display/EPC on marketing:
  - Scotland: an EPC must be available to prospective tenants/buyers and certain sellers/landlords must display the EPC rating in commercial property adverts.
- Exemptions/heritage:
  - Both have limited exemptions, but criteria and processes differ (e.g., Scottish “special considerations” for technically/architecturally sensitive buildings).

Section 63 Action Plan (Scotland)
- What it is: An additional regime under the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009 and Non-Domestic Buildings (Scotland) Regulations 2016 aimed at reducing carbon and improving energy performance beyond the EPC.
- Trigger: When a non-domestic building (or building unit) over 1,000 m² is offered for sale or let and the EPC is being provided. Certain building types are exempt (e.g., some industrial sites, workshops, temporary buildings, places of worship).
- Process:
  - A Section 63 Advisor (accredited) assesses the building using the EPC outputs.
  - If triggered, the owner must either:
    1) Implement prescribed improvement measures within 42 months and lodge a completed Action Plan, or
    2) Opt to adopt and maintain a Display Energy Certificate (DEC) with an associated improvement report and annual renewal, instead of immediate physical measures.
- Interaction with EPC rating: Section 63 is separate from the EPC band; it’s about specific improvement measures or ongoing operational performance via DEC.
- Enforcement: Local authorities can enforce; penalties apply for non-compliance (e.g., failure to lodge an Action Plan or DEC when required).

Does MEES apply in Scotland?
- No. The MEES (Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards) regime, which restricts letting sub‑E EPC properties unless exempt, is specific to England & Wales (and a separate regime exists for NI). Scotland has not adopted MEES for non-domestic properties.
- Practical implication: In Scotland you can legally let a property with a low EPC rating, but you may still be required to comply with Section 63 if the building is ≥1,000 m², and prospective tenants will see the EPC.

Practical steps for a Scottish landlord marketing a commercial property
- Ensure a current Scottish EPC is lodged and available at marketing.
- Check net floor area. If ≥1,000 m² and not exempt, engage a Section 63 Advisor:
  - Decide between implementing measures within 42 months or adopting a DEC route with annual renewals.
- Confirm any specific exemptions (e.g., temporary buildings, places of worship, demolition candidates).
- Note that MEES does not restrict letting in Scotland, but market expectations may still pressure improvements.

Here’s what’s currently set out for heat network regulation under the UK Energy Act 2023 and Ofgem’s developing framework, relevant to a new scheme going live in 2027:

- When authorisation becomes mandatory
  - The Energy Act 2023 establishes a formal authorisation (licensing-style) regime for heat networks, but the provisions require secondary legislation and Ofgem implementation before they bite.
  - Government and Ofgem have indicated a phased commencement from 2025–2026, with full authorisation requirements expected to become mandatory once the authorisation scheme is switched on by secondary regulations. For a scheme commissioning in 2027, you should plan on needing an Ofgem heat network authorisation in place before supplying customers.
  - Existing networks will get transition arrangements; new networks coming online after commencement are expected to need authorisation from day one.

- Who the regulator is
  - Ofgem is the statutory regulator for heat networks under the Energy Act 2023. It will administer authorisations, monitor compliance, enforce standards, and set/oversee price regulation where directed.

- Key consumer protections that will apply
  The Act creates a framework allowing government to set detailed rules through secondary legislation and Ofgem licence/authorisation conditions. The core protections expected include:
  - Customer standards and service quality: minimum service standards, performance reporting, guaranteed standards of performance (e.g., for outages, complaint handling, response/repair times), and redress/compensation for failures.
  - Transparency and information: clear pre‑contract information, standardized heat supply agreements, clear billing formats, consumption information, and notice of price changes.
  - Pricing and value for money: Ofgem powers to regulate pricing and profits, including potential price caps or principles‑based price regulation to protect customers from unfair or excessive charges.
  - Vulnerable customers and disconnection protections: safeguards for priority/vulnerable consumers, rules on disconnections and cooling‑off rights, and support for those in payment difficulty.
  - Complaints and redress: mandatory participation in an independent Alternative Dispute Resolution scheme; Ofgem enforcement powers and consumer redress orders.
  - Technical and reliability standards: requirements for metering/heat cost allocators, reliability and resilience standards, outage reporting, and maintenance obligations.
  - Switching and network changes: protections during operator changes or significant network events, and continuity-of-supply requirements.
  - Data and privacy: rules on use of consumption data and smart/metering data protections.

What to do now for a 2027 go‑live
- Engage early with Ofgem’s authorisation guidance and consultations; design commercial documents (heat supply agreements, tariffs, billing) to align with expected conditions.
- Build in processes for customer service standards, outage response, complaints/ADR, vulnerable customer support, and transparent pricing.
- Ensure metering/monitoring systems can meet data and billing transparency requirements.
- Plan for potential price regulation and associated reporting.

Note: Final timelines and detailed conditions depend on forthcoming secondary legislation and Ofgem’s final decisions. Check BEIS/Department for Energy Security and Net Zero and Ofgem updates as they are published to confirm commencement dates and detailed rules.

Here’s a concise summary based on the Energy Act 2023 (Part 8: Heat Networks) and associated government policy statements as they stand up to June 2026.

1) Powers of a heat network zone coordinator
- Core role: A designated zone coordinator (expected to be a local authority or another body appointed for the area) identifies potential heat network zones, coordinates planning and delivery, and exercises statutory functions conferred by regulations made under the Act.
- Likely functions (subject to secondary legislation):
  - Prepare, propose, and manage heat network zones, including data gathering, mapping, and assessment.
  - Issue zoning decisions and administer local consents relevant to heat networks within the zone (to the extent provided by regulations).
  - Require the provision of information from building owners, heat suppliers, network operators and utilities to support zoning and enforcement.
  - Coordinate connections: identify “relevant buildings” and oversee requirements to connect where the statutory test is met.
  - Procurement/market facilitation: run competitive processes to appoint zone delivery bodies or concessionaires; enter into agreements enabling development and operation of heat networks in the zone.
  - Enforcement and penalties: monitor compliance and use enforcement tools (notices, penalties) created by regulations for failures to connect or provide information.
  - Interface with licensing/consumer protection: liaise with the national heat networks regulator (Ofgem) and apply any licensing or permitting conditions relevant within the zone.
Note: The Act is an enabling framework. The detailed powers and procedures (e.g., exact notice formats, appeals, penalty levels) depend on secondary legislation made by the Secretary of State.

2) Which buildings can be required to connect
- The Act enables mandatory connection in designated heat network zones for “relevant premises” defined by regulations. Government policy indicates mandatory connection will target:
  - Large, high and constant heat‑demand buildings, typically:
    - Larger non-domestic buildings (e.g., hospitals, universities, large offices, leisure centres).
    - High‑heat multi‑residential buildings (e.g., high‑rise blocks, large apartment schemes) where technically and economically viable.
  - New developments within a zone, where connection can be designed in from the outset.
- Key constraints (as signalled by the Act and policy):
  - Viability tests: connection can only be required if technical and economic assessments show it is cost‑effective and suitable.
  - Exemptions/deferrals: buildings may be exempted (e.g., on heritage/technical grounds) or granted deferrals (e.g., recent low‑carbon plant, disproportionate costs, or where network capacity is not yet available).
  - Phasing: requirements may apply at defined trigger points (e.g., at boiler replacement, major refurbishment, or by a specified date).
- Gas grid: The government has indicated it will consult on and provide a route to manage interactions with existing gas supplies and avoid “double regulation,” but forced disconnection from gas will be handled via specific regulatory steps, not automatically by zoning alone.

3) Commencement status as of June 2026
- Primary legislation: The Energy Act 2023 is in force, but the heat network zoning regime relies on secondary legislation. As of June 2026:
  - Zoning provisions are not yet fully commenced for operational rollout nationwide. The government has been preparing detailed regulations for:
    - Appointment and functions of zone coordinators.
    - Methodology for designating zones.
    - Classes of buildings subject to mandatory connection and the tests/exemptions.
    - Enforcement, appeals, data‑sharing, and interaction with planning and other regimes.
  - Pilots and preparatory work: Government and local authorities (including West Midlands/Birmingham through earlier pilots) have been undertaking preparatory mapping and market engagement, but mandatory connection powers and formal zoning duties await the secondary legislation coming into force.
- Regulator: Ofgem’s role as heat networks regulator is being phased in via separate commencement regulations, focusing first on consumer protection and licensing; full alignment with zoning will occur once the zoning regulations commence.

Practical takeaway for Birmingham city centre in mid‑2026:
- You can prepare and consult on a proposed zone, gather data, and line up delivery structures.
- However, the statutory powers to mandate connections, issue enforcement notices, and run formal zoning appointments depend on the forthcoming zoning regulations. Until those commence, any connections must be achieved via planning conditions/obligations, procurement, and voluntary commercial agreements rather than the Act’s mandatory-connection mechanism.
